explored.angle: Self-organising and developmental differentiable systems: neural cellular automata (NCA), graph and developmental NCAs, differentiable logic CA, Lenia-family agents, and meta-learned local rules. The question is how one shared local rule, trained by gradients (BPTT on a GPU), by evolution, or by both, could replace the GRN+LIF cell while keeping growth, death, one life per body and multidirectional circuits. Grounding: I read RESULTS.md, docs/POST_PILOT_CALLS.md, docs/HARDWARE_PATH.md and docs/BODY_DESIGN_PROPOSAL.md (SPECK/CATCH-T rules, surface-normal pull, reflex@hollow3 +8.69 against s5 +7.06, s5 earning 9.65 with 115 cells). Two small timing checks are in the scratchpad: alt/ncadev/bench.py (bit-sliced logic rule) and alt/ncadev/bench_nca.py (dense hex NCA step in torch). Verification: every paper below was opened at its URL. The Science Advances DOI for Sensorimotor Lenia returned 403, so it is cited through the lab's page. The WebSearch budget was already used up when I started, so I could not search for 2025-2026 work beyond what I fetched directly. In particular I did not find, and so cannot rule out, any published NCA that grows a body and steers it within one life.

candidates.name: Grow-and-Act NCA (GA-NCA): one shared neural rule per lattice site, trained by gradient through whole lives
candidates.one_liner: Replace the GRN+LIF cell with one small neural network that every site runs (a neural cellular automaton). It grows the body, carries the messages and drives the dot, and is trained by backprop through continuous lives on a GPU, with population-based evolution choosing among lineages.

candidates.unit: Each site of the existing hex-prism lattice holds a vector of C = 16-32 real channels. One channel is 'alive'. Two or three channels are a polarity vector: the cell's own 'front'. The rest are free channels, each with a learned leak rate, so the rule decides for itself which channels are fast (membrane-like) and which are slow (gene-like); no GRN/LIF split is fixed in advance. The update is state += mask * f_theta(own state, the 8 face messages received, the receptor input at its screen point). f_theta is a small MLP shared by all cells (the genome): in the timed configuration, 4.8k parameters and 4.7k multiply-adds per site per step. Its last layer starts at zero, so a new rule 'does nothing' at first (Growing NCA). There is no type table: cell types appear as stable states of the shared rule, as differentiated cells do in NCAs.
candidates.communication: Every step, a cell writes a separate small vector (M about 4) to each of its 8 faces, and the neighbour reads it on the next step. Messages are directional, but the law is isotropic: the message on a face is computed from the angle between that face and the cell's polarity vector, as steerable/isotropic NCA perception does. 'Excite upward, inhibit downward' then becomes a direct readout instead of the fragile morphogen-gradient construction the pilot found, which cost s5 -10.10 F when made isotropic. Timing: synchronous steps, but each cell updates with probability 0.5 per step, and training adds 0-2 steps of random delay per edge, so the rule cannot rely on lockstep. Several message micro-steps per world time unit give faster conduction, which the pilot found helps every body. Optional binary mode: messages pass through a spike nonlinearity trained with surrogate or straight-through gradients.
candidates.learning: Inner loop (within life): the forward dynamics only. Cells adapt through their slow channels, as genes do now. Candidate 4 adds true within-life learning. Outer loop, gradient: truncated BPTT through the tissue and a torch re-implementation of SPECK. A hard capture disk gives zero gradient almost everywhere, so training needs either a soft-edged capture disk (edge width about 0.2), a score-function gradient for the click probability, or a critic used only during training. Evaluation always uses the real Poisson world with a hard disk. 'Pool' training keeps lives continuous: 1,024 persistent lives, each advanced 32-64 steps per update and written back, and replaced by a zygote when it reaches T. Every life is therefore one zygote-to-death life, trained in windows. Outer loop, evolution: Population-Based Training. 8-16 lineages are trained in parallel. Periodically the worst copies the best one's weights and perturbs hyperparameters: costs, channel count, delay noise, leak priors. Selection then works between lineages and gradient within each lineage, which also gives several concurrent breeds instead of the pilot's collapse to one lineage by generation 2-119.
candidates.growth: Mitosis is one fixed op: when a cell's 'divide' output is positive, it copies its state, with a ±asym split, into the empty face that its direction output picks relative to its polarity. Alive below 0.1 means death. A per-cell living cost and a per-message cost in the loss bound growth without a size target, the same cost structure as now. Keeping what was learned small: the rule does not depend on body size, so it is trained first at R_cap 1-2 and short lives, then the cap and world difficulty are raised and the same theta continues. The rule's own capacity grows without changing its function, the analogue of gene duplication. New channels start with zero writes; a duplicated hidden unit takes half of the outgoing weights, as in Net2Net. Behaviour is identical at the moment of growth, and then the copies diverge.
candidates.circuitry: Any directed recurrent circuit along lattice paths. Each face carries its own vector, so a cell can relay, gate, invert or merge signals in any direction. Feedback inhibition loops, latches and lateral voting are ordinary. Long-range links still need relay chains, but micro-steps make chains fast. It does not allow arbitrary graph edges; candidate 2 does.
candidates.hardware: GPU-native: one step is 8 shifted reads and one batched MLP. Measured on this laptop CPU (torch, 12 threads, 900 sites, 4.8k parameters): 6.9 ms per step for 32 lives, or 222 ms per 1,024-step life [M]. That is slower per life than the C kernel's ~100 ms. A 4090-class GPU estimate: 8.7 GFLOP per life forward, so roughly 1-3k lives/s forward and about 3x fewer when training [E]. Raw throughput is therefore about that of one 192-core box, and the gain is gradient information per life (a direction in ~5k dimensions from each batch), not lives per second. Computing only live cells instead of the dense box cuts the dense waste about 5-9x at pilot body sizes [E]. Later hardware: an int8 per-cell MLP, or compiling the rule to logic gates (candidate 3). Training under the 0.5 update mask prepares the rule for an asynchronous array.
candidates.evidence: Growing NCA: 16 channels, about 8k parameters, a 50% random per-cell update 'to avoid global synchronization' (each cell 'waiting for a random time interval'), pool training and regeneration. Self-classifying MNIST: cells agree on a body-wide label through local messages only (95.4% peak accuracy, 88.1% agreement at 200 steps). NCA cart-pole: an NCA trained by DQN controlled stably for thousands of steps and tolerated input deletion. 3D NCA: structures of more than 3,000 blocks, and regrowth of functional machines. Regenerating soft robots: an NCA regrew damaged bodies, which partly regained locomotion. Sensorimotor Lenia: CA creatures with about 130 parameters, trained by gradient with a goal curriculum, navigate obstacles and stay robust to asynchronous updates, scale changes and damage. IsoNCA: rotation-invariant rules, with symmetry broken by the seed or by asynchrony. Shared modular policies and DGN: one shared per-module policy with message passing steers different bodies and generalises to unseen ones. NoiseNCA: NCAs can learn continuous dynamics that survive changes of time step. Gap: I found no published system that grows a body and steers it within one life with bounded growth.
candidates.risks: (1) Long horizons. Gradients over 1,024+ steps explode or vanish, and NCAs drift; mitigations are pool training, short windows, state noise and gradient clipping. (2) A differentiable world is needed. A soft capture edge or a critic is a training device, not the fitness, but it presses against the standing 'no shaped score' call, so the real world must stay the only judge. (3) Lockstep exploits such as synchronous oscillation. Async masks and delay jitter are mandatory, plus a transfer gate in an asynchronous simulator. (4) Real-valued messages lose the value-less spike discipline, so message cost must be redefined (e.g. L1 on message magnitude). (5) Discrete growth decisions get no gradient. This works in Growing NCA but may slow growth learning; PBT or evolution covers it. (6) Gradient descent converges fast to one solution; PBT and a quality-diversity archive are needed for diversity. (7) It will not make hidden layers useful if the task gives depth no job, which was the pilot's finding.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: re-implement SPECK in torch: dot physics, surface-normal pull, receptor rates at training time and Poisson events at test time, soft click. Build the hex-prism NCA (13x13x4 box, C 16, M 4, about 5k parameters). Check the world port by encoding the hand-built reflex as a fixed rule; it must give the C kernel's F within noise. Week 2: pool BPTT on one rented L4 or 4090 for 1-2 days, PBT with 8 lineages, curriculum R_cap 1, then 2, then 3. Week 3: evaluate in the real world with common random numbers, and run the async gate (fully random-order asynchronous updates plus delay jitter). Success: F at least the re-tuned reflex@hollow3 with no more than its cell count (the pilot was 0 of 10); at least 90% of F kept under asynchronous inference; growth stops with no size cap; lesioning lateral messages costs more than 50% of F. Budget: about 10-50 GPU-hours.
candidates.relaxes: The global clock: training uses steps and treats asynchrony as noise. It is worth it because that is what unlocks dense GPU ops and BPTT, and the async gate tests whether behaviour depends on lockstep. Value-less spikes: messages are real vectors, with a binary mode optional. No gradients: it uses them. It keeps one continuous life (pool training), local rules, growth, death, energy costs and bounded growth.

candidates.name: Developmental graph tissue: cells that grow their own directed wires, with function-preserving division (NDP/LNDP-style)
candidates.one_liner: Cells still sit on the body lattice, but they grow and prune directed, weighted, delayed edges to cells within a radius. Division copies a cell Net2Net-style, so the circuit's function is unchanged at the moment it divides. Shared node, synapse and growth rules are evolved with GPU-batched evolution strategies, plus plasticity within the life.

candidates.unit: A cell is a node with a GRU state h (16-32 values) and a lattice position, so the BODY-1 physics and sensing stay as they are. A synapse is a directed edge with its own small state: weight, eligibility trace, age. Three shared networks form the genome, about 3-8k parameters in total. (a) The node GRU. (b) An edge plasticity rule, dw = g_phi(pre, post, eligibility, local modulator). (c) Growth heads: divide, a wire-seeking query/key, and prune. Every cell and every edge uses the same parameters, as in Structurally Flexible NNs, so the genome does not grow with the body.
candidates.communication: Small vectors travel along directed edges. An edge's delay is its length divided by a conduction speed, in integer steps, so long wires are slow and are paid per unit length; this matches BODY-1's planned 'radius gene paid per wire length'. It can run stepped on a GPU, or event-driven, sending only when a node's output changes by more than a threshold. Wiring by local attention: a node's seek query is scored against the keys of nodes within radius R (e.g. 3 lattice units). The top-k (k at most 8-16) become edges, and edges whose |w| stays low are pruned. Edges are directed, so A->B and B->A are independent.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: evolution strategies on the GPU (OpenAI-ES or CMA-ES, ask/tell over a vectorised population, antithetic pairs and common random numbers) over the shared parameters. ES folds the fitness of thousands of perturbations into one update, which tolerates per-life Poisson noise better than the current truncation selection (pilot reliability 0.026 per life). A GA stage can keep separate breeds. Inner loop (within life): reward-modulated edge plasticity and structural plasticity, preceded by a 'spontaneous activity' phase with random sensory firing before the task starts (LNDP), so the wiring self-organises while the body is small. A differentiable NDP trained with PPO is possible (Najarro 2023 compare both), but discrete edge and node growth favours ES.
candidates.growth: Division duplicates a node Net2Net-style. The daughter copies the mother's incoming edges and state, and mother and daughter each take half of the mother's outgoing weights. The tissue therefore computes exactly the same function right after a division, and plasticity or the next generations then make the pair different. This is the most literal mechanism for 'what was learned small is kept, then extended'. Growth stops through costs per node, per unit of edge length and per message. Death removes the node and its edges. As in the current project, evolution can start from a 1-2 cell founder and lengthen lives and raise R_cap over time.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary directed graphs: recurrent loops, long-range skips, convergence and divergence, hubs. None of them need to relay through every lattice site, which attacks the pilot's diagnosis that the routing gap is earnings per cell. The radius R keeps it local enough to map onto hardware. Weights are per edge, so direction-specific weighting needs no morphogen chemistry.
candidates.hardware: GPU: padded node and edge arrays per life (N_max 128-256, E_max about 16 x N_max), gather/scatter segment sums, and computation only for live cells. That is roughly 0.3-1 GFLOP per 1,024-step life, so several thousand lives per second on one GPU [E], vectorised across the ES population. Gather/scatter runs less efficiently than dense ops. FPGA/ASIC: a node is a small recurrent core, and edges of bounded radius map to a mesh network-on-chip. The event-driven variant maps onto neuromorphic chips (spike packets on a network-on-chip) better than a lattice NCA does.
candidates.evidence: NDP: a 162-parameter evolved NDP grew a 10-node, 33-edge network that solves CartPole (500 ± 0 over 100 rollouts). An 868-parameter NDP grew 16 nodes and 78 edges for LunarLander at 116 ± 124, below the 200 'solved' mark. The differentiable NDP reached 91% on 8x8 MNIST, and in their tables more growth steps sometimes made performance worse. LNDP: evolved graph-transformer rules with synaptic and structural plasticity plus a spontaneous-activity phase learn control tasks starting from empty or random networks, and structural plasticity helps where adaptation must be fast or rewards change. HyperNCA: an NCA grows policy weights, and its 'metamorphosis' variant adapts the weights to task variants. Structurally Flexible NNs: one evolved set of GRU neurons and plastic synapses solves several control tasks with different input/output sizes. Hebbian meta-learning: random-start networks with evolved rules adapt to body damage within about 100 steps. Graph CA and E(n)-equivariant GNCA: learned transition rules on arbitrary graphs, with locality and isotropy. Net2Net: function-preserving widening and deepening. Scale caveat: all of these are around 100 nodes or fewer, and none grow a body that senses at its surface.
candidates.risks: (1) The evidence is small-scale and modest; LunarLander was not solved. (2) Edge growth can explode or collapse to all-to-all, so it needs costs and degree caps, and each cap is a hard-coded rule to justify. (3) ES still needs many lives, though they are batched on the GPU, and its gradient estimate in about 5k dimensions is noisy. (4) GPU efficiency is lower than dense NCA ops. (5) Two learning loops (evolution plus plasticity) are hard to debug, and evolution may simply switch plasticity off. (6) Wires weaken the 'only physical neighbours talk' bio constraint, so R should stay small and be paid per length.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: graph tissue in torch (house style; JAX with evosax is the alternative) on BODY-1 lattice positions, N_max 128, out-degree at most 8, R = 3, Net2Net division. Unit test: a forced division leaves all outputs unchanged up to float rounding. Week 2: OpenAI-ES on SPECK on one GPU (population 2,048 antithetic, 2 common-random-number lives each, 300-500 generations). Week 3: lesions (drop edges between non-neighbours; freeze plasticity), compared with candidate 1 and with the GRN pilot at equal dollars. Success: F at least reflex@hollow3. Earnings per cell above s5's (9.65 with 115 cells). Edges between non-neighbours carry at least 30% of F. Freezing plasticity costs F in a world that varies per life (e.g. receptor sign or motor gain redrawn each life).
candidates.relaxes: Messaging only through lattice contacts: grown wires replace it. The clock, if run stepped on a GPU; an event-driven version is natural and keeps clocklessness. Spikes are optional (vector messages). It keeps one continuous life, growth, death, locality within radius R and evolution as the main learner.

candidates.name: Logic tissue: differentiable-logic CA cells with binary spike messages, compiled to exact gates
candidates.one_liner: Each cell is a few dozen bits plus a learned circuit of ~300-1,500 two-input logic gates shared by all cells. The circuit is trained by gradient in a relaxed form, hardened to exact Boolean logic, then refined by evolution in an asynchronous simulator. It is the paradigm closest to running natively on hardware.
inspiration: Miotti, Niklasson, Randazzo, Mordvintsev (2025) Differentiable Logic Cellular Automata, Google Research. https://google-research.github.io/self-organising-systems/difflogic-ca/
Petersen, Borgelt, Kuehne, Deussen (2022) Deep Differentiable Logic Gate Networks, NeurIPS. https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08277
Petersen, Kuehne, Borgelt, Welzel, Ermon (2024) Convolutional Differentiable Logic Gate Networks, NeurIPS. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04732
Mordvintsev, Niklasson (2021) muNCA: Texture Generation with Ultra-Compact Neural Cellular Automata. https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13545
Mordvintsev, Randazzo, Niklasson, Levin (2020) Growing Neural Cellular Automata (asynchronous-update rationale). https://distill.pub/2020/growing-ca/
candidates.unit: A site holds B = 32-64 bits: alive, divide and direction bits, 1-2 'spike-out' bits per face channel, a 3-4 bit counter that plays the membrane, and some free 'gene' bits. The update is a learned circuit of two-input gates shared by all cells: a perception part plus an update part. During training each gate is a soft mixture over the 16 two-input Boolean functions (probabilistic relaxation). Afterwards each gate is hardened to its most likely function, which yields an exact, inspectable Boolean rule.
candidates.communication: 1-2 bits per face per update: value-less spikes, as now (2 channels). Neighbours read them at their next update. Updates are asynchronous: each cell updates at its own random times, using masks in training and a per-cell Poisson clock in inference. DiffLogic CA reports that synchronously trained rules still worked under asynchronous inference, and that asynchronous training improved robustness to perturbations.
candidates.learning: Gradient first: the relaxed circuit is trained by BPTT in the same pool / continuous-life setup as candidate 1. Alternatively it is distilled from a trained candidate-1 rule as a teacher (match its messages and actions), which makes the logic circuit a compile target. Evolution second: after hardening, mutate gate functions and input wires (Cartesian-GP-style point mutations) and evaluate in an exact asynchronous or event-driven simulator. Gradient makes the large moves; evolution makes the discrete fine-tuning and handles everything non-differentiable, such as growth decisions. Inner loop: none beyond the state bits, which can act as switchable modes.
candidates.growth: The same alive and divide bits drive one fixed mitosis op (copy state into the chosen empty face). The rule grows without changing its function: append gates whose outputs feed in through identities (OR with 0, AND with 1), so behaviour is unchanged until training or evolution uses them. Rules do not depend on grid size: DiffLogic CA rules generalised to 4x larger grids and 4x longer runs, so the train-small, deploy-large curriculum applies.
candidates.circuitry: Any directed recurrent circuit along lattice paths, through per-face bits (as in candidate 1 but binary). The logic is exact and readable as Boolean formulas, which suits the project's habit of dissecting how evolved bodies work.
candidates.hardware: The best fit of the four. Measured with numpy bit-slicing (64 lives per uint64 word; 900 sites x 1,000 random gates x 1,024 steps): 42.6 G gate-evals/s on ONE laptop core including Python overhead, or 21.6 ms per life [M], against roughly 100 ms per life for the current C kernel. A C/AVX2 or GPU integer version should be several times faster again [E]. On an FPGA or ASIC each gate becomes a LUT or standard cell. A 1k-gate rule is a small combinational block plus a register, and per-cell asynchronous clocks make it exactly the long-term 'local logic natively on hardware' target. The bit-exact software rule is the reference, which fits the integer ABI plan in HARDWARE_PATH.md.
candidates.evidence: DiffLogic CA: learned Game of Life (336 active gates); a checkerboard (5-6 essential gates after pruning) that generalised to 4x larger grids and 4x longer horizons; growth of a 20x20 lizard with 577 gates, reconstructed on 40x40; a colored G with 927 gates; asynchronous inference worked. Its stated limitation: complex patterns needed extensive hyperparameter tuning. Deep DLGN: more than 1M MNIST images/s on one CPU core. Convolutional DLGN: 86.29% on CIFAR-10 with 61M gates, 29x smaller than prior work. muNCA: NCAs as small as 68 parameters still work for textures, so tiny rules are expressive. I found no published DiffLogic agent, control or growth-plus-behaviour result (search budget limited).
candidates.risks: (1) Hard to train (the authors report heavy tuning), and control through a world is harder than matching a pattern; distillation from candidate 1 is the fallback. (2) Hardening can change behaviour, so only the hardened rule may be evaluated. (3) Integrating over time and graded gains must be built from bits and counters, which may need many gates. (4) No within-life learning beyond state. (5) Synchronous-training artefacts unless asynchronous masks are enforced.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: a bit-sliced hard-logic tissue simulator (C, or torch integer ops) on the hex-prism lattice, plus a relaxed DLGN in torch. Sanity checks: reproduce DiffLogic CA growth of a small fixed shape, and train a 2-cell 'sense here, click here' reflex. Week 2: distil the hand-built reflex, and a candidate-1 rule if one exists, into at most 2k gates; in parallel, train on SPECK directly with relaxed gates. Week 3: harden, evolve gates in an exact asynchronous simulator, measure. Success: the hardened body keeps at least 90% of its relaxed or teacher F in the real Poisson world under fully asynchronous updates, at 10x or more fewer CPU-s per life than the current kernel.
candidates.relaxes: The clock during training only (asynchrony applied as masks). The continuous membrane becomes bits and counters. It keeps value-less spikes, locality, growth, death and one life, and is closest to the hardware goal and the no-lockstep preference.

candidates.name: Learning tissue: two-stream cells that meta-learn a local learning rule (VSML/BLUR inside the NCA)
candidates.one_liner: Give every cell (or every face-synapse) a tiny shared recurrent unit with a forward activity stream, a backward feedback stream and fast weights. Meta-train it across many lives and world variants, so the grown tissue learns within its life with no global gradient, and new cells arrive already able to learn.
inspiration: Kirsch, Schmidhuber (2021) Meta Learning Backpropagation And Improving It (VSML), NeurIPS. https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14905
Sandler, Vladymyrov, Zhmoginov, Miller, Jackson, Madams, Aguera y Arcas (2021) Meta-Learning Bidirectional Update Rules (BLUR), ICML. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04657
Plantec, Pedersen, Montero, Nisioti, Risi (2024) Evolving Self-Assembling Neural Networks (LNDP). https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09787
Najarro, Risi (2020) Meta-Learning through Hebbian Plasticity in Random Networks, NeurIPS. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.02686
Zhang, Risi, Darlow (2025) Petri Dish Neural Cellular Automata, Sakana AI. https://pub.sakana.ai/pdnca/
candidates.unit: The candidate-1 cell plus (a) fast-weight state on each face (the synapse), which changes during the life, and (b) a feedback channel group. The shared parameters, about 1-3k, are the genome and never change during a life; learning in life lives entirely in the state (fast weights). This is VSML's 'tiny shared LSTM at every connection' placed in a grown tissue.
candidates.communication: Two messages per face per step, a forward one (activity) and a backward one (feedback, running opposite to activity), plus one neuromodulator that diffuses from a reward receptor (e.g. the click cell senses capture or miss). BLUR shows backprop is the special case of such a two-state network, so this channel can carry error-like signals if evolution or meta-training finds that useful.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: meta-learning across many lives and world variants. Gradient through short lives (128-256 steps) on a GPU, or ES for long lives. Inner loop: the forward dynamics implement learning. Within one life the body discovers, for example, which receptor sign means 'target' or how its motors map onto movement, which a fixed reflex cannot do when these are redrawn every life. This is the version of 'learn local optimizations' that happens during the life itself, not only over generations.
candidates.growth: New cells instantiate the same learner. Fast weights start fresh or copied from the mother (Lamarckian within the life), so adding cells adds learning capacity without retraining the genome. Meta-train on small bodies and deploy on larger ones; VSML and BLUR report learned rules that generalise beyond their training tasks.
candidates.circuitry: Any lattice-path circuit as in candidate 1, or any graph as in candidate 2, with plasticity along both directions of every link.
candidates.hardware: Per step it costs about 2-3x candidate 1 (more state per face). The real cost is meta-training: nested loops and BPTT over lifetimes need a GPU, while inference is as local as candidate 1. On chip, fast weights are local registers per face, so it remains a processor array.
candidates.evidence: VSML: tiny shared LSTMs at every connection meta-learn learning algorithms that generalise to datasets outside the meta-training distribution and work differently from gradient descent. BLUR: neurons with two or more states and a shared low-dimensional genome of bidirectional Hebb-like rules, meta-learned (including by CMA-ES), generalise to unseen tasks and on some tasks train faster than gradient descent. LNDP and Hebbian meta-learning: evolved local plasticity adapts within an episode. PD-NCA: NCAs that keep learning by backprop during the simulation produce cyclic and cooperative dynamics; without learning the dish goes static. All of this is small-scale, and none of it is in a grown body.
candidates.risks: Meta-training is unstable and expensive. Evolution or meta-training may ignore the learner and solve the task with a fixed reflex unless worlds vary per life. Credit assignment over long gaps is weak. Hard to interpret. It adds one fixed rule (the reward receptor and modulator) that needs a justification.
candidates.prototype: After candidate 1 exists (weeks 2-3): add the feedback channels and fast weights per face. Build worlds where receptor sign or motor polarity is redrawn every life, so a fixed rule cannot win. Meta-train with BPTT over 256-step lives on one GPU. Success: a within-life learning curve (captures in the last third greater than in the first third), beating the best fixed-rule NCA trained on the same world distribution, and working unchanged on a 2x larger body.
candidates.relaxes: As candidate 1 (clock, real-valued messages), plus one broadcast or diffusing modulator. It adds true within-life learning, which the GRN only approximates through gene-expression changes. There is still no global gradient within a life.

explored.cross_cutting:
1. **Suggested order.** Build candidate 1 first as the base: the torch SPECK port, pool training, the async gate and PBT are reused by candidates 3 and 4. Candidate 3 is then the 'compiler' target (continuous NCA, then logic gates, then FPGA), and candidate 4 is an add-on. Candidate 2 is the alternative to try if relay chains on the lattice remain the bottleneck on earnings per cell.

2. **Be honest about throughput.** A dense NCA is not faster per life than the C kernel (222 ms per life on the laptop CPU [M]; about one 192-core box per GPU [E]). What gradients buy is information per life: a direction in ~5k dimensions from each batch, instead of a noisy rank among 1,000 lives that gives ~0.005 F per generation. Bit-sliced logic is faster per life (21.6 ms per life on one core with Python overhead [M]).

3. **Evolution and gradient together** (Baldwinian or Lamarckian, PBT). Evolution chooses among lineages, hyperparameters and breeds, and keeps a quality-diversity archive on behaviour descriptors (size, share of fitness that is lateral, growth stop time). Gradient does the local optimisation inside each lineage. This answers 'each child ~0.19 F worse than its parent' and the collapse to one lineage.

4. **Continuous life without giving up batching.** Pool training keeps persistent lives that are advanced in windows and written back, so every life runs from zygote to death and is trained piecewise. The same trick lets ES or GA evaluate long lives in GPU batches.

5. **Clock independence as a test, not a simulator constraint.** Train with random per-cell update masks, per-edge delay jitter and variable step size (NoiseNCA shows NCAs can learn step-size-robust dynamics). Then require at least 90% of F when the trained rule runs in an asynchronous referee: each cell updates at its own Poisson times, built from the existing window scheduler or a Gillespie loop. That keeps the user's 'behaviour must not depend on lockstep' while allowing dense GPU training.

6. **Function-preserving growth at two levels.** Body: Net2Net division (the daughter copies incoming edges or face weights and takes half the outgoing ones). Genome: new channels or gates enter with zero or identity effect, and duplicated hidden units split their outgoing weights. This is gene duplication that never breaks a working body. Self-Expanding Neural Networks (Mitchell, Menzenbach, Kersting, Mundt 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04526) adds a natural-gradient test for when to add capacity.

7. **Train small, deploy large.** Shared rules do not depend on size. DiffLogic CA generalised to 4x grids and times, Sensorimotor Lenia to scale changes, and Mesh NCA (Pajouheshgar et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02820) to unseen meshes. Use R_cap, life length and world-difficulty curricula, and later move the same rule to the cursor-following and text-stream worlds through the same sense plane.

8. **Polarity instead of morphogens for direction.** Give each cell a heading vector (like planar cell polarity) and make perception steerable relative to it: isotropic in law, directional in practice (IsoNCA, https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01681; E(n)-GNCA, https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10497). This is the NCA-world version of the post-pilot 'per-channel face weights', and it separates synapse sign from division placement, which the morphogen gradient currently ties together.

9. **Lower-noise objectives that are not shaped.** Train on expected rather than sampled quantities where the world allows it: receptor rates instead of Poisson events, click probability instead of a sampled click. Use a critic only during training. Always judge on the real Poisson world with common random numbers. ES with antithetic pairs plus CRN averages per-life noise over thousands of perturbations.

10. **Give depth a job.** No paradigm will use hidden layers if the task is solvable by a one-hop reflex (the pilot's hidden_off result). Pair any new substrate with worlds that need memory or integration: an occluded or delayed cursor, a sign redrawn each life, a text stream.

11. **Keep the exact clockless kernel and still get gradients.** EventProp (Wunderlich, Pehle 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.08378) computes exact gradients for event-driven LIF networks by the adjoint method, with no time grid. It could train face weights and gains inside the current C kernel for a fixed grown morphology, leaving growth to evolution. It is a large engineering lift because the GRN and division events are discrete.

12. **One continuous world, longer term.** Flow-Lenia (Plantec, Hamon, Etcheverry, Oudeyer, Moulin-Frier, Chan 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07906) keeps total mass constant and carries rule parameters inside the matter, so several species with different rules evolve inside one simulation. PD-NCA (https://pub.sakana.ai/pdnca/) has NCAs learning online while they compete. Both point to bounded growth by conservation instead of tuned costs, and to evolution inside one long world rather than over generations of separate lives.

13. **Tooling.** CAX (Faldor, Cully 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02651) reports CA simulations up to 2,000x faster than traditional implementations. evosax (Lange 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04180) has 30 GPU-vectorised ES algorithms. Within the torch house style, torch.func.vmap plus a hand-written OpenAI-ES is enough.

explored.angle: Local learning rules and meta-learned plasticity: cells that keep learning inside one life, so what they learn while the body is small is copied, consolidated and reused as it grows. Evolution (or meta-learning) tunes the learning rule, not every weight. Grounded in the repo's findings: direction-specific synapses exist only through a costly, fragile morphogen route (s5 loses 10.1 F when isotropic); hidden planes are inert; each child is about 0.19 F worse than its parent; per-life F has an SD of about 2.0; apoptosis is unused; the cell struct already stores weff[DMAX][2] per face and channel (src/life/kernel.c:201, summed on spike arrival at :1063). Web search was exhausted for this session, so every source below was checked by opening its arXiv, Europe PMC or Crossref record directly. Ackley & Littman 1991 could not be verified.

candidates.unit: Today's cell: LIF membrane plus the shared 16-gene GRN, with one genome for every cell. Added to each contact face d (up to 8) and channel c (2): a plastic offset p[d][c] (Q8), a presynaptic trace x[d][c], an eligibility e[d][c] (Q16), and one postsynaptic trace y per cell. The effective weight becomes w_eff[d][c] = q8((w_c + o_face(d),c + p[d][c]) * (1 + a_c*shat_d)), a superset of the proposed X1 face weights. The rule has a fixed generic form and evolved coefficients. When a spike arrives through face d on channel c: x += 1, e -= A_minus*y. When the cell fires: y += 1, and e[d][c] += A_plus*x[d][c] for every face and channel. All traces decay exponentially between events. The weight changes as dp = eta0*(instant STDP term) + etaM*M*e - lambda*(p - u), with a slow consolidated copy u <- u + (p - u)/tau_c (a Benna-Fusi style two-variable synapse). About 6 new GRN readout rows set eta0, etaM, the A-/A+ ratio, a tau_e bucket, lambda/tau_c and modulator release. Evolution therefore decides which cells learn, when (critical periods arise from GRN state, not a schedule), and with what sign. An inhibitory-channel option uses Vogels' homeostatic rule.
candidates.communication: Unchanged: value-less spikes on 2 channels to up to 8 neighbours, about 1 time-unit delay, asynchronous and event-driven, plus the slow morphogen packets. Added: one diffusing modulator scalar M, carried in the same TICK packet machinery as the morphogens (a third amt/conc field). The task outcome enters only locally. A capture is a sensory event at the hotspot site, like a receptor ping, and the GRN decides whether that cell (or any other) releases modulator. There is no global reward broadcast, so evolution evolves its own taste.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: the existing (32+224) GA with crossover evolves the GRN and the rule coefficients. It is Baldwinian: learned weights are never written back to the genome. Inner loop: local two-factor STDP that shapes wiring from spike timing, plus three-factor learning (eligibility x diffused modulator) for reward-dependent tuning, plus optional homeostatic inhibitory plasticity. Because the rule is shared and has few parameters, what evolution tunes on small bodies is size-agnostic. Pedersen & Risi found that fewer shared rules generalise better.
candidates.growth: At division the daughter copies the mother's p[d][c], u[d][c] and trace state, indexed by absolute lattice direction. No rotation is needed on the hex-prism lattice. So a learned 'excite from below, inhibit from above' profile, or a crowding-tuned gain, appears in every new column without re-learning: an epigenetic, within-life Lamarckism. Consolidation (u) makes old cells' weights stiff while young cells stay plastic, so growth adds capacity without overwriting. GRN-gated plasticity can close a cell's learning window as it matures. An inheritance-off fork measures whether copying matters.
candidates.circuitry: Any recurrent nearest-neighbour graph, as now. Plasticity can make each contact effectively unidirectional, bidirectional, excitatory or inhibitory per face and per channel. Clopath et al. 2010 show timing-coded activity drives predominantly unidirectional connections. Long range still needs relays or the planned radius gene.
candidates.hardware: CPU: stays exact and event-driven. Traces decay analytically between events (Morrison et al. 2008), and every update depends only on the receiving cell's own events, so the window scheduler (each site advances alone, a fence every h <= d_min) remains exact. Extra state is about 64 numbers per cell. Estimated cost is +10-30% CPU per life (not measured). GPU: still a poor fit, unchanged. FPGA/ASIC: the best fit of all four candidates. Trace-based local and three-factor learning is what on-chip learning silicon does: Loihi's learning engine, and ReckOn's e-prop at 0.45 mm2, under 150 uW of training power and 0.8% memory overhead. Q8 weights plus Q16 eligibility fit the planned integer ABI 4, though eligibility increments may need at least 10 fractional bits; the gene state already does.
candidates.evidence: Najarro & Risi 2020: synapse-specific Hebbian rules (more than 450K plasticity parameters) starting from random weights let a quadruped learn to walk and adapt to unseen damage in under 100 timesteps without a reward signal. Pedersen & Risi 2021: cutting the rules from 61,440 to 1,920 parameters improved robustness across 30 unseen morphologies. Jordan et al. 2021: evolution rediscovered gradient-like and STDP-like spiking rules for reward and supervised learning. Confavreux et al. 2025: ES meta-learned co-active rules for all four E/I synapse types in recurrent spiking nets, with many degenerate solutions. Miconi 2023: evolved neuromodulated plastic nets acquire cognitive tasks never seen in evolution. Hinton & Nowlan 1987: learning makes evolution much faster even without inheritance (the Baldwin effect). A project-specific prediction: the evolved bodies fire sense to act about 1.0 time unit apart, and act-to-sense feedback arrives after the sense spike. Pair STDP therefore potentiates from-below inputs and depresses from-above inputs, the exact profile every SPECK body built from chemistry. Song et al. 2000 and Clopath et al. 2010 support timing-driven unidirectionality. This prediction is not yet tested here.
candidates.risks: (1) The excitable sense sheet can run away: s5 depends on feedback inhibition. Confavreux found stability is the hardest constraint, so include homeostatic or inhibitory plasticity and a weight clip. (2) In a stationary world evolution may set the learning rates to 0, so plasticity needs within-life variation (the L2 epoch worlds or the L1 family) to pay, unless it pays as self-wiring. (3) It adds one fixed rule form and per-contact memory, which conflicts with docs/DOWNSTREAM.md M9's 'no synapse memory' pitch. The justification: at zero coefficients it is bitwise ABI 3/4, it replaces a morphogen route costing about 10% of s5's running cost, and silicon learning engines show the memory is small. (4) Selection noise remains, and in-life learning curves add variance. (5) Exactness: weight updates at exact ties must follow the kernel's tie contract, and the hashes must fold the new state. (6) In Najarro-style systems the 'learning' is sometimes fast self-organisation that then freezes. That is still useful here, but it must be measured, not assumed.
candidates.prototype: Week 1 (reference.py first, then kernel.c): add the plastic offsets with a plastic_off fork; golden tests prove bitwise ABI 3 at zero coefficients. Hand-set test with no evolution and under 1 CPU-h: take the s5 and s4 bests, knock out chemical direction (a_c = 0, which costs s5 -10.1 F), and switch on pure STDP at 3-5 hand-set (A+, A-, tau) settings, 256 paired CRN lives each. Success: STDP rebuilds up-excite/down-inhibit within about 100 time units and recovers at least 50% of the lost F. Weeks 2-3: SPECK matrix with 3 arms (ABI 3; X1 static face weights; plastic faces) x 10 seeds x 500 generations, about 720-940 CPU-h, about 5 h on one 192-core spot box (about $15-35, estimated from the pilot audit). Success: (a) the plastic arm's median F is at least the static arm's; (b) freezing weights at birth costs at least 1 F in at least 5 of 10 bests; (c) the existing 40-mutant test gives a mean child drop below s5's 0.19 F (Baldwin buffering); (d) capture retention over the four shifted worlds is at least the reflex's 0.58; (e) the inheritance-off fork costs F in bodies that grow after the learning has settled.
candidates.relaxes: Keeps no global clock, one continuous life, spikes, locality and the shared genome. Relaxes the 'no per-contact synaptic memory' hardware stance and adds one fixed rule form (trace STDP x modulator, coefficients evolved). Worth it because direction-from-chemistry is costly and breaks when the gene clock changes, and this route is the most hardware-native of the four.

Meta-train them with ES on GPUs over a task family so the tissue must learn within its life; growth copies state.

candidates.unit: The genome is two tiny shared recurrent networks. The first is a cell program (a GRU with a 16-32-float state, replacing GRN + membrane) run in every cell. The second is a synapse program (a GRU with a 4-8-float state) run on every contact face. Both are conditioned on a few type genes; per SFNN, several neuron and synapse types break the 'symmetry dilemma' of identical shared units. That is about 2-10k shared parameters in total, the same for every cell. A division head on the cell state outputs p_div and a direction, and an optional death head. The existing GRN is already a shared tiny RNN; the differences are that this one runs on synapses too, sends real-valued messages that can carry learning signals, and is meta-trained over many tasks.
candidates.communication: Each step every contact carries a forward vector (k = 2-4) from pre to post and a backward vector from post to pre. The backward vector is the channel VSML uses to implement credit assignment inside the network. A diffusing modulator is added. Time-stepped (for example dt = 0.25 world units), with a random asynchronous update mask (each cell updates with probability p per step, as in NCA training) so behaviour cannot rely on lockstep.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: ES (OpenAI-ES, PGPE or CMA via evosax) on the shared parameters, vmapped over population x lives x worlds on one GPU. Meta-train over a task family (SPECK variants, sensor permutations and sign flips, speed switches within a life) so that remembering one world cannot win and learning inside the life is required. Optionally use truncated meta-gradients through the differentiable parts. Inner loop: no explicit gradient. Whatever the cell and synapse states do is the learning algorithm. VSML shows such programs can run backprop in forward mode, and can also find different, fast-association algorithms that generalise outside the meta-training distribution.
candidates.growth: Daughters copy the mother's cell state and the synapse states of the faces they inherit, so knowledge learned while small is carried into new tissue. The programs are size-agnostic: SFNN shows one evolved set of units working across different input/output sizes. Use a size curriculum: meta-train on 7-19-cell tissues, then 37 and above, keeping the same parameters. Structural plasticity (making or pruning contacts, apoptosis) can be activity- and reward-dependent, as in LNDP, where structural plasticity helped under fast adaptation and non-stationary rewards.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary: every contact is bidirectional with typed vector messages, recurrent loops are allowed, and longer range comes through relays, a radius gene, or LNDP-style attention over a small neighbourhood.
candidates.hardware: GPU/TPU-native: dense [pop x lives x cells x faces x state] tensors on a padded fixed lattice with alive masks, as in NCA work. Thousands of lives per step. EvoJAX reports minutes on one accelerator for tasks that took hours or days on CPU. Later ASIC: one small MAC engine per cell plus per-face state RAM, a systolic-array-like tile. Links are wider than 1-bit spikes. After meta-training, try binarised or event-gated messages to recover spike-like economy.
candidates.evidence: VSML (NeurIPS 2021): tiny shared LSTMs in place of weights implement backprop in forward mode and meta-learn new learning algorithms that generalise beyond the meta-training distribution. SymLA: adding symmetries to black-box meta-RL improves generalisation to unseen action/observation spaces and environments. SFNN 2024: one set of GRU neuron and synapse types solves several RL control tasks with different I/O sizes. LNDP 2024: self-organising networks learn control tasks from random or empty starts, with pre-experience spontaneous activity. BLUR 2021: meta-learned Hebb-style bidirectional rules generalise to unseen tasks. Cautionary: VeLO needed about 4,000 TPU-months for a general learned optimiser. Small-scale VSML/SFNN work is far cheaper, but meta-training cost is the main risk.
candidates.risks: (1) Meta-training cost and ES variance over 1,000+ step unrolls. (2) A black box: harder to dissect than GRN + LIF, which threatens the probe-toolkit style of interpretation (though GRUs this small can be lesioned). (3) It relaxes the clock and spikes. (4) It may solve tasks by in-context state tracking rather than durable learning; test with mid-life state freezes and world switches. (5) The symmetry dilemma: identical units in identical positions stay identical without noise, types or positional cues. (6) Dense stepping wastes compute on silent cells. (7) The selection-noise problem remains, but GPU throughput allows averaging 32-64 lives per genome. (8) It moves away from the event-driven hardware path the project has invested in.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: port SPECK (dot, receptor pings, twitch, tap) to JAX, time-stepped. Fidelity gate: the hand reflex scores within about 5% of the kernel's +8.69 at some dt. This also answers the hardware study's open question of which dt leaves behaviour unchanged. Week 2: a fixed hex disk of 19 sites x 2 planes, no growth; cell GRU 16, synapse GRU 4, messages 2+2. OpenAI-ES with population 512 x 32 lives on one rented H100, an estimated $2-4/h and $100-300 in total. Week 3: add the division head and grow from 1 cell; meta-train at 19 cells and test at 37. Success: (a) beats the re-tuned reflex in the JAX world; (b) the program trained at 19 cells keeps at least 90% of its score at 37 without retraining; (c) after a mid-life sensor sign flip, the score recovers to at least 70% of its pre-flip level within about 200 time units, while a state-frozen fork does not.
candidates.relaxes: Relaxes the clock (time-stepped, with randomised asynchronous masks as mitigation) and spikes (graded vector messages). Meta-training also favours many shorter lives, though each evaluation can still be one continuous life. Keeps locality, the shared genome and growth. Worth it because it uses GPUs fully, and it is the only candidate where the learning algorithm itself is discovered rather than given a fixed form.

candidates.name: C. Predictive tissue: every cell minimises its own prediction error (a predictive-coding graph, optionally spike-coded on the two channels)
candidates.one_liner: Give every cell a local objective, predicting its own input from its neighbours, with predictions and errors flowing in opposite directions on each contact. Learning is local and Hebbian and runs continuously. Inserting a zero-weight cell does not change the function, and evolution sets what is predicted, how precisely and how fast.

candidates.unit: Each cell holds an activity estimate mu and computes a local error eps = mu - f(sum_d w_d * mu_d), the gap between itself and what its neighbours predict for it. Its activity relaxes to reduce pi*eps^2 plus the errors it causes in its neighbours (local energy descent). Per-face weights learn by dw_d proportional to pi * eps_self * f(mu_d) (local Hebbian). Its GRN sets: precision pi (the gain on error), learning rate, whether the cell is clamped to its receptor (sense cells) or drives twitches (act cells), and an optional prior (an expected value, for example the hotspot cell expecting 'tap followed by capture'). A spiking variant keeps LIF cells and codes eps and predictions as spike rates or timing on the two existing channels.
candidates.communication: Two message types on every contact: predictions in one direction, errors in the other. That maps onto the two existing spike channels (for example ch0 = error spikes, ch1 = prediction spikes), or onto graded values in a time-stepped version. Payeur et al. show one spike train can also multiplex events and learning signals through bursts. Inference is energy descent, so asynchronous update orders converge to the same fixed point, though transients still depend on order.
candidates.learning: Inner loop: incremental PC (iPC), where inference and weight learning run at the same time and continuously, with no phases, which fits one continuous life. Learning is local and Hebbian and, in some limits, matches backprop (Whittington & Bogacz). Outer loop: the GA evolves the GRN, deciding growth, which cells are clamped, precisions, learning rates and priors. Evolution therefore chooses what the tissue predicts, and acting to reduce prediction error (active-inference style) produces behaviour. Fitness stays the task score, which guards against degenerate predictors.
candidates.growth: Function-preserving by construction. A new cell whose outgoing prediction weights are 0 changes no other cell's prediction or energy minimum (a Net2Net-like insertion); its weights then learn. Daughters copy the mother's weights. Older cells can raise precision and lower their rate (evolved consolidation). Hidden planes get a job, predicting the sense plane, so a small body's learned sensory model stays in place as layers are added above it.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary graphs including cycles. PC graphs (Salvatori 2022) run inference and learning on any topology, and choose the task by which neurons are stimulated. Every contact is bidirectional by construction.
candidates.hardware: A time-stepped version is dense and batches on GPUs. The spiking version runs in the existing event-driven kernel, with error and prediction spikes as events. Energy-based learning is a leading candidate for analog substrates: Equilibrium Propagation targets analog hardware, C-EP is local in space and time, and holomorphic EP gets exact gradients from finite oscillations. That fits the project's long-term native-hardware goal.
candidates.evidence: Whittington & Bogacz 2017: local Hebbian PC approximates backprop. Salvatori 2022: PC learns on arbitrary and cyclic graphs. Song et al. 2024 (Nat Neurosci): 'prospective configuration' learns more efficiently than backprop in biologically relevant settings and reproduces human and rat data. iPC 2022: stable, phase-free PC with good accuracy on image and language benchmarks. Ororbia 2019: spiking PC with reduced forgetting on data streams. EP: CIFAR-10 at 11.7% error (Laborieux 2021), and ImageNet 32x32 matching backprop with holomorphic EP (2022). The evidence is mostly supervised and static; closed-loop control at scale is weaker.
candidates.risks: (1) Unproven for fast closed-loop control. The world needs answers within about 1 time unit, while PC often needs many relaxation steps per input; iPC helps. (2) The 'dark room' problem: a surprise-minimising tissue can learn to avoid targets. Task-score selection and evolved priors must hold purpose in place. (3) A fixed objective ('predict your input') is a hard-coded rule. The justification: it gives the inert hidden planes a job, and prediction is the core of the planned LEAD, mouse-following and text-stream tasks. (4) Coding signed errors with spikes is awkward. (5) If the prediction loss dominates, the tissue may model the world well and act poorly.
candidates.prototype: Week 1, time-stepped Python/JAX with no evolution: a 2-plane hex tissue whose sense plane is clamped to SPECK receptor pings from a moving target, with a hidden plane above, running iPC in one continuous life. Success: a linear readout of the hidden plane predicts target position 2-5 time units ahead better than a persistence baseline on held-out speeds. Growth test: adding a ring of cells mid-life causes no jump in prediction error, which then falls further. Weeks 2-3: add the act plane, with act-cell errors driving twitches. The GA searches the GRN rows (precision, rate, prior, clamp) in SPECK and in a LEAD-like world where the target passes behind an occluder. Success: beats the re-tuned reflex in the LEAD-like world by at least 3 SE, the gate already written in POST_PILOT_CALLS L4, and a hidden-plane knockout costs F. Compute: a laptop or one GPU, days.
candidates.relaxes: The first version relaxes spikes (graded values) and partly the clock (relaxation steps; robust to update order only at fixed points), and adds a hard-coded local objective. Keeps one continuous life (iPC is online), locality and growth. Worth it for the later prediction-heavy tasks and because it is the most principled way to make depth useful.

candidates.unit: Same as candidate A: an LIF cell with GRN-set plasticity coefficients and per-face plastic weights. In the twin, spikes use a surrogate derivative, and the GRN tick and morphogen diffusion are stepped at a fixed dt.
candidates.communication: The organism keeps value-less spikes, delays and asynchrony in the exact kernel. Only the twin is time-stepped, so the clock exists only in the training tool, not in the organism that gets scored.
candidates.learning: Outer loop, two parts. (i) Meta-gradients (BPTT or backpropamine-style, truncated) through the twin optimise the continuous shared parameters: rule coefficients, modulator gains and GRN readout rows. The loss is a de-noised expected-capture objective, the expected F given the trajectory rather than the Poisson-sampled F, run on many lives in parallel. (ii) The GA keeps the discrete and developmental choices (division genes, placement, growth stop) and applies selection using exact-kernel F only. Inner loop: candidate A's local three-factor rule, or e-prop with an evolved local learning signal.
candidates.growth: The same as candidate A: inheritance and consolidation of learned weights. Growth itself is not differentiated through, because division is discrete; mature-body snapshots are used as fixed twins between generations.
candidates.circuitry: The same as candidate A: any nearest-neighbour recurrent graph, with direction and sign learned per face.
candidates.hardware: The GPU twin batches like any time-stepped SNN. Evolving Connectivity (Wang 2023) ran large recurrent SNN populations on GPUs with 2-3x efficiency gains over parameter evolution. The exact CPU kernel stays the referee and the hardware contract. The final rule runs natively on event-driven or neuromorphic silicon, as in candidate A.
candidates.evidence: Differentiable plasticity and Backpropamine: gradient-trained plastic and neuromodulated networks with millions of parameters solve memory, meta-learning and language-model tasks. LSNN L2L: spiking networks learn to learn via gradient outer loops. e-prop: online local learning that approaches BPTT in recurrent SNNs, including reward-based learning. Shervani-Tabar & Rosenbaum, and Lindsey & Litwin-Kumar: meta-learned local rules with random feedback match or beat online gradient learning, especially in continual learning. Confavreux 2020: gradient and ES meta-learning recover known plasticity rules.
candidates.risks: (1) The twin-kernel gap. Time-stepping changes behaviour, and the hardware study notes that the dt which leaves behaviour unchanged is unmeasured. (2) Gradients over 1,000+ steps of spiking dynamics explode or vanish; truncation biases them. (3) An expected-capture loss is a smoothed objective. POST_PILOT_CALLS rejected a shaped score because it breeds parking near targets, so the kernel referee must veto twin gains that do not show up in real F. (4) Two code paths to maintain. (5) The gradient optimiser is global, but only in the outer loop, where the GA is equally global.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: a JAX twin of fixed, non-growing mature bodies (s5, s4, the reflex) at their end size. Measure the twin's F against the kernel's F as a function of dt (0.25 down to 1/32). This is a useful deliverable on its own. Week 2: on the twin, start from s5 with chemical direction knocked out and meta-learn candidate A's rule coefficients by truncated BPTT. Compare against GA on the same parameters at equal wall-clock. Week 3: move the best rules into the exact kernel. Success: (a) kernel F within 1 SE of the twin's prediction for at least 8 of 10 transferred parameter sets; (b) the gradient arm reaches the GA arm's final F in at most 1/5 of the wall-clock; (c) no parking signature (time near target up while captures fall).
candidates.relaxes: The organism keeps every preference: clockless, one life, spikes, local learning. The training tool relaxes the clock (a lockstep twin), and the outer loop uses gradients and a de-noised loss. It is worth it because the measured bottleneck is noisy, slow GA progress (late gains of about 0.005 F per generation, shortlist rank correlation about 0.03), and gradients on expected F attack exactly that.

explored.cross_cutting:
1) "Timing teaches direction": a cheap, decisive test. Every SPECK body builds "excite from below, inhibit from above" out of a morphogen gradient, at about 10% of s5's running cost, and the route breaks when the gene clock is 4x slower. Sense-to-act spikes arrive about 1.0 time unit apart, and act-to-sense feedback lands after the sense spike, so plain pair STDP should learn that profile from timing alone (Song, Miller & Abbott 2000, https://doi.org/10.1038/78829; Clopath et al. 2010, https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.2479). The test needs no evolution: a_c = 0 plus hand-set STDP on s5, 256 paired lives. If it works, both X1 face weights and the chemistry route become optional.

2) Five mechanisms for "learn small, keep it when big", usable in any candidate:
- (a) Evolve shared, few-parameter rules rather than weights; they transfer across size. Fewer rules generalise better (Pedersen & Risi 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07959), and SFNN units transfer across I/O sizes (https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.15193).
- (b) Copy the learned per-face state into daughters at division: within-life epigenetic inheritance.
- (c) Consolidate locally with a fast/slow two-variable synapse (Benna & Fusi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4401) or importance-weighted stiffness (Zenke, Poole & Ganguli 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04200; Kirkpatrick et al. 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00796). The importance is computed from the synapse's own history, so it stays local.
- (d) Let the GRN gate plasticity, so critical periods emerge rather than being scheduled.
- (e) Insert new units without changing function: zero-weight insertion (Net2Net, https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641; a PC cell with zero outgoing predictions), with new cells absorbing new demands (Draelos et al. 2016, Neurogenesis Deep Learning, https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.03770).

3) Give death a job. Continual learners lose plasticity unless low-utility units are re-initialised (Dohare et al. 2024, Nature, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07711-7). Apoptosis of cells whose synapses carry little eligibility or use, followed by regrowth through the existing claims, is the tissue analogue. Apoptosis never fires in any evolved body today.

4) Use the Baldwin effect against the measured selection problems. Learning smooths the landscape and speeds evolution (Hinton & Nowlan 1987, https://www.complex-systems.com/abstracts/v01_i03_a06/). Plastic tissue can partly repair mutational damage. Measure it with the existing 40-mutant protocol: s5's mean child drop is 0.19 F, with 0 of 40 better, plasticity on versus off. Expect only an indirect effect on Poisson score noise; the gradient twin (D) or GPU-scale averaging (B) attack the noise directly.

5) Evolve the reward rather than hand-coding it. A capture should arrive only as a local sensory event at the hotspot, and the GRN should decide whether to turn it into a diffusing modulator. This is the "evolutionary reinforcement learning" idea of Ackley & Littman, 1991, Artificial Life II; I could not verify a URL for it. Miconi 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08588) shows evolved neuromodulated plasticity learning tasks never seen in evolution.

6) Plasticity pays only when the life contains surprises. Make the planned epoch worlds (L2) or the per-life task family (L1) a prerequisite. Standard probes for every candidate: freeze weights or state at mid-life; recovery after a world switch; transfer across body sizes; inheritance off; plasticity off during development only.

7) Rank learning signals by how local they are, and prefer the most local that works:
- spike timing or homeostasis (fully local);
- local prediction errors (C);
- a diffused modulator times an eligibility trace (A);
- random-feedback broadcast (e-prop; needs a broadcast, so diffuse it).

The two spike channels can carry a signal and its learning signal, as bursts do in Payeur et al. 2021 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-021-00857-x), rather than only excitation and inhibition.

8) Hardware alignment. Trace-based local and three-factor rules are what on-chip learning silicon implements: Loihi (https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2018.112130359) and ReckOn (https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09759). Reserve Q8 weights and Q16 traces in the integer ABI 4. Receiver-local updates keep the window scheduler exact.

9) Two-fidelity workflow for any candidate: a GPU time-stepped twin (EvoJAX https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05008, evosax https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04180) for screening and meta-learning, and the exact clockless kernel as the referee whose F alone selects. Its first deliverable is the twin-versus-kernel F curve over dt, which the hardware study lists as unmeasured.

10) Degeneracy is normal. Many different rules give the same behaviour (Confavreux et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.05.28.656584; PLoS CB 2025, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012910). Judge rules by behaviour and robustness, and expect crossover between unrelated lineages' rule coefficients to work poorly.

Suggested order:
- A first: cheapest, and keeps every standing preference.
- D if GA progress stays the bottleneck.
- C when LEAD, mouse or text tasks arrive and depth needs a job.
- B as the long bet on GPU-scale meta-learning.

explored.angle: Networks that grow and evolve their topology while keeping what they have already learned: function-preserving growth (Net2Net, network morphisms, GradMax, SENN, splitting descent, masked growth), the NEAT family and CPPN encodings, developmental encodings (cellular encoding, NCA/NDP), gene and module duplication with divergence, and continual-learning expansion (progressive nets, PathNet, MoE upcycling). The question throughout: how can a small body learn local computations, then grow without losing them, keeping arbitrary recurrent circuitry? Context from the repo: the pilot's main costs were (a) each child is about 0.19 F worse than its parent, so mutation is mostly destructive, (b) Poisson selection noise, (c) direction-specific synapses had to be built from morphogen chemistry, (d) hidden planes went unused, and (e) there is no within-life learning beyond gene expression. Each candidate below says which of these it targets. Some sources I could only check at the metadata or abstract level, and each citation says so. The session's web-search budget ran out early, so all verification was done by fetching known URLs (arXiv, DOI, Crossref, Semantic Scholar).

candidates.unit: A cell holds its GRN gene state g (16 genes, as now) plus a membrane/hidden state h (8-32 numbers) and a maturation gain a in [0,1] on its outgoing messages. One cell program theta_cell, the same in every cell like an NCA, maps (h, g, inbox, local senses) to (new h, an outgoing message per face, divide/die/secrete drives). It is a small GRU or 2-layer MLP of about 1-5k parameters. Every directed contact (up to 8 faces on the hex-prism) stores its own weight w and an eligibility trace e. A shared synapse rule theta_syn updates them with a three-factor Hebbian law, dw = eta * m * (A*pre*post + B*pre + C*post + D), where the coefficients come from both endpoints' gene states. This gives direction-specific synapses on every edge without morphogen gradients. In the pilot, making s5's weights isotropic cost -10.1 F, and its chemistry broke at a slower gene clock. This is the per-face weight idea (X1) taken to its end.
candidates.communication: Per-edge messages: a scalar or a small vector, or binary spikes trained with straight-through/surrogate gradients. Topology is the lattice contacts, so any local recurrent circuit can form, and direction comes from the per-edge w. The GPU advances in fixed steps dt, but at each step only a random subset of cells updates (per-cell probability p, as in Growing NCA and DiffLogic CA), and per-edge delays are jittered. Evolved behaviour therefore cannot rely on lockstep. Winners are certified by replaying them at several p and dt and, for a spiking variant, in the existing exact event-driven C kernel.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: the current GA, or GPU evolution strategies over theta_cell, theta_syn and the GRN. Populations of thousands become affordable, which attacks Poisson selection noise directly: 64-256 CRN lives per genome cut the standard error 8-16x. Inner loop, within one life: edge weights learn by the evolved three-factor rule. The third factor is a local neuromodulator released at capture events (or by sense cells on reward) that decays and diffuses like a morphogen, so learning stays local and clock-free. Gene-expression changes continue as now. An optional ML shortcut: pre-train theta_cell by backprop through development and behaviour on a smooth proxy world, the way Growing NCA was trained by BPTT, then evolve on true F. Selection always uses true F; the pilot showed shaped scores breed parking near targets.
candidates.growth: Division places the daughter in an empty neighbouring site as now, and the asym*Q partition stays as the symmetry breaker. To keep function: (1) the daughter's outgoing gain a starts at 0 and ramps up under her own GRN, as a silent newborn that matures in. This is the same idea as masked structural growth, GAN fade-in and adult-born neurons integrating gradually. (2) Her incoming weights copy the mother's learned per-face table, rotated by the face offset, so the learned local computation is inherited. At the moment of division the tissue's output is exactly unchanged, so growth is neutral by construction instead of a gamble. Graph variant, if cells may also grow edges to non-neighbours: a Net2Net split, where the daughter copies all of the mother's in- and out-edges and both halve their out-weights, which is exact. Feed the GRN one new local input, a 'conflict' signal: the cell's eligibility-weighted learning-signal variance, a cheap stand-in for the splitting-matrix test of Liu et al. 2019, which splits a neuron sitting at a saddle. Whether to divide on it is left to evolution, not hard-coded.
candidates.circuitry: Any recurrent circuit that can be laid out on the 3D lattice: loops, feedback inhibition, lateral voting and latches (all found in the pilot), now with learned direction on each edge. Long-range wiring needs relay chains, or the graph variant, where cells extend edges to non-neighbours by following local guidance cues (NDP-style).
candidates.hardware: GPU now: B lives x N sites (at most 1024, as a padded dense 3D grid) x 8 faces. Each step is a gather over 8 neighbours plus one batched small matmul with the shared theta_cell, the classic NCA shape (Conv3D or gather + bmm), all dense and runnable in bf16/fp16. Rough estimate [E]: 1,024 lives x 1,024 sites x about 5k MAC per cell update is about 5 GMAC per step; at about 2k steps per life that is about 1e13 MAC per generation, seconds to tens of seconds on one L4/A10-class GPU, against about 100 CPU-s per generation today. Not measured. Later FPGA/ASIC: one small fixed datapath per site, replicated. HARDWARE_PATH found fixed point fitness-neutral for the GRN, and the window scheduler already shows exact per-site parallelism for the event-driven variant. A logic-gate cell (DiffLogic CA) would be the most chip-native form.
candidates.evidence: Growing NCA grows and regenerates patterns from one cell with a shared per-cell network trained by BPTT and stays stable under random asynchronous updates. DiffLogic CA learns discrete gate rules (Game of Life, patterns) with randomized updates, and they work on larger grids. HyperNCA and NDP grow policy networks by local developmental programs. LNDP adds activity- and reward-dependent synaptic and structural plasticity within a life on control tasks. Najarro & Risi evolved per-synapse Hebbian rules that learn locomotion from random weights within a life and recover from damage. MSG and Progressive GAN show that masked or faded-in growth keeps function (MSG reports up to 2.2x faster LM pre-training). Net2Net's split is exact. Scales are small (tens to thousands of nodes, Gym/MuJoCo-class control), and I found no work combining neutral division, per-edge plasticity and evolution on a moving-body task.
candidates.risks: (1) Graded messages and lockstep training may yield solutions that break in the clockless kernel; schedule randomization and cross-checks are mandatory. (2) Evolved plasticity can blow up weights, so it needs bounds or homeostasis, and such rules are known to be hard to evolve. (3) Meta-gradients through thousands of development steps are long-horizon and chaotic, needing truncated BPTT or ES only. (4) The shared program has thousands of parameters against the 250-number genome today, so plain GA mutation could get more destructive; ES with large populations fixes this but changes the evolutionary flavour. (5) Silent newborns might never mature into use, so maturation must stay under GRN control and be measured.

candidates.unit: Node: an LIF or rate neuron (or a tiny GRU) with its own tau, threshold and bias, plus a type id. Edge: (src, dst, weight, delay of 1..D steps, plastic flag), tagged with a NEAT innovation number. Direct encoding: no shared parameters, though optional node types can share parameters as a light indirect layer. Sensors and motors are nodes bound to body receptors and twitch actuators.
candidates.communication: Directed weighted edges between any two nodes, so any recurrent or multidirectional circuit can form. Delays use ring buffers. Messages are spikes (surrogate gradients) or rates. Training advances in lockstep dt. Asynchrony can be approximated during evaluation with per-edge random delays and update masks.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: NEAT-style evolution of topology and hyperparameters (learning rate, which edges are plastic). Speciation protects new structure, and historical markings align genomes for crossover. Selection is on true task F over many parallel GPU environments. Inner loop, per child: K steps of training by one of three routes: (a) BPTT with surrogate gradients through a smooth relaxation of the world; (b) policy gradient or actor-critic on the true world; (c) e-prop, which is online and local (eligibility traces plus a broadcast learning signal) and is the most hardware-native. Lamarckian: trained weights are written back into the genome, as in Real et al. Baldwinian control arm: the genome keeps its pre-training weights.
candidates.growth: The mutation set is made of morphisms. Add-node-on-edge (NEAT: in 1, out = old weight; exact for near-linear rate units, approximate for LIF). Split-node (Net2WiderNet: duplicate and halve outgoing weights; exact while the copies agree). Add-edge at weight 0 with GradMax direction (function unchanged, largest initial gradient). Duplicate-subgraph (copy a module and halve its outputs; exact): the duplication-divergence operator. Prune and regrow (SET / Deep R). Where to grow comes from local triggers computed from a node's own activity and learning signal: the splitting matrix (Liu et al. 2019), the natural expansion score (SENN), or activation orthogonality (NORTH). Start from a minimal sensor-to-motor graph and add hidden nodes only where they reduce loss, which targets the pilot's inert hidden planes.
candidates.circuitry: Fully arbitrary directed graphs with cycles and delays. No geometry is needed; optional node coordinates allow a wiring-length cost, which promotes modularity (Clune, Mouret, Lipson 2013).
candidates.hardware: TensorNEAT pads graphs to a fixed maximum size and reports up to 500x over NEAT-Python on GPU. For N up to 256 nodes, each step is a dense masked N x N matvec (or block-sparse), batched over population x environments. BPTT memory is T x N x batch, fine with truncation; e-prop needs only O(edges) traces. Estimate [E]: 256 genomes x 64 envs x (256x256) x 1,000 steps is about 1e12 MAC per forward rollout, seconds on one GPU, so a 100-step inner loop takes minutes per generation. Later hardware: a trained sparse SNN maps to neuromorphic routing tables or a fixed-point FPGA design, and e-prop was designed with on-chip learning in mind.
candidates.evidence: NEAT: minimal start, complexification and speciation on control tasks. Real et al. 2017: weight inheritance across structural mutations reached 94.6% on CIFAR-10. Elsken et al. 2017: hill climbing with morphisms plus short training reached under 6% CIFAR-10 error in 12 GPU-hours. Gesmundo & Dean 2022: evolutionary growth with parameter inheritance over 69 image tasks. Net2Net, Network Morphism, GradMax, SENN and Firefly: growth that keeps learned function speeds up training. e-prop: local online learning in recurrent SNNs approximating BPTT. Deep R: sparse rewiring including spiking RNNs. I did not find work combining Lamarckian morphism-NEAT with recurrent spiking graphs on an embodied task; morphisms are best established for feedforward nets, CNNs and transformers.
candidates.risks: (1) It drops the developmental 'genetic code': the genome is the network itself (direct encoding), which scales poorly past a few thousand nodes and loses 'one genome grows the tissue'. Mitigations: node types, or nesting candidate A/D inside. (2) Gradients through spikes over long horizons are fragile, and Poisson capture rewards are not differentiable, so training needs a proxy loss. That risks the 'parking' failure if the proxy leaks into selection, so selection must stay on true F. (3) Lamarckian inheritance can speed up the collapse to one lineage the pilot already shows, so speciation or QD is needed. (4) Morphisms are only approximately function-preserving for LIF thresholds; measure the birth deficit. (5) It is the least bio-like option and trains on a clock.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: torch padded recurrent graph (N_max 128, E_max 1024), LIF with surrogate gradient, delays of 1-4 steps, batched dot-chase world. Week 2: morphism mutations (split, add-node, zero-edge, duplicate-subgraph) and NEAT speciation; inner loop of 50-200 Adam steps on a smooth proxy (expected capture probability); selection on true F over 64 CRN lives. Week 3: four arms at equal GPU-time: Lamarckian + morphisms, Lamarckian + random-init mutations, Baldwinian, and pure evolution with no inner loop (today's regime). Compute: 2-4 GPU-days. Success: the Lamarckian + morphism arm gains at least 3x more F per GPU-hour than pure evolution; birth deficit about 0 against today's about -0.19 F per child; the best graph beats the re-tuned reflex; hidden nodes carry at least 20% of F by knockout.
candidates.relaxes: Relaxes the global clock (lockstep training), the single continuous life (many training episodes per generation, though it could be framed as one long life with continual learning), developmental/indirect encoding (replaced by direct morphing) and, initially, spikes. Keeps arbitrary recurrence and, with e-prop, local learning. Worth running as the 'best-case ML' reference: it measures how much of the gap to the reflex is search efficiency rather than model expressiveness, which tells you how much A, C and D can hope to gain.
