candidates.unit: Module: a small dense recurrent block (LIF or GRU, 8-64 units) with K input and K output ports. Its genome is either its weights (direct) or a seed from which a mini-tissue grows (candidate A inside the module). Each module carries a lineage id recording which module it was copied from, which supports NEAT-style alignment and crossover at the module level.
candidates.communication: Between modules: sparse directed channels carrying small vectors or spike bundles with delays. Any module can connect to any other, in any direction. Each module has its own input gate, a local router (a gate or attention over its incoming channels), so 'which expert listens to what' is decided locally, not by a central MoE router. Timing is GALS (globally asynchronous, locally synchronous): lockstep inside a module, timestamped messages with random delays between modules. That is a deliberate compromise on the no-clock preference, and it matches multi-core chips.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: evolution over the module graph (which module to duplicate, where to wire the copy, which modules to protect), with innovation numbers per module. Inner loop: gradient or e-prop, or evolved plasticity, inside modules. Protection: old modules get low plasticity or are frozen (Progressive nets, PathNet), while new copies are plastic. On a new task rung, branch copies, train them in parallel on parts of the new task (BTX), then merge them as experts behind local gates.
candidates.growth: Duplicate a module: copy its weights, and gate the copy's outputs with a maturation gain ramping from 0 to 1 (or halve both copies' outputs, which is exact). The copy inherits the original's input channels and may take new sensor channels. Two routes to divergence: subfunctionalization, where the copies split the old job (e.g. left and right halves of the screen; the DDC model of Force et al.), or neofunctionalization, where the copy takes a new input or task while the original keeps the old one. Developmental version within cell-dev: duplicate a progenitor cell's state before it differentiates, and its whole lineage, an organ, is duplicated. That is segment duplication, and it links to the pilot finding that reflex arcs are lineages.
candidates.circuitry: An arbitrary module-level graph with cycles, plus arbitrary recurrence inside modules, which gives hierarchical modularity. A wiring cost encourages modules to stay modular (Clune et al. 2013).
candidates.hardware: GPU: modules are batched dense GEMMs (grouped GEMM / MoE kernels, block-sparse), and inter-module messages are a sparse gather. 8-64-unit blocks use the hardware well, much better than per-neuron sparse graphs. Chip: one module per core on a network-on-chip, the way SpiNNaker/Loihi-style multi-core designs are built, with GALS timing. Module granularity matches a tile and avoids per-neuron routing tables.
candidates.evidence: Biology: module and pathway duplication are proposed routes to new function (Calabretta 2000 in evolved networks; Chakraborty & Jarvis 2015 for vocal learning; Arendt 2016 for sister cell types; Force 1999 for gene subfunctionalization). ML: PathNet freezes learned paths and evolves new ones, with positive transfer on supervised and RL tasks. Progressive nets avoid forgetting through lateral connections. Gesmundo & Dean grew a multitask system over 69 tasks with inheritance and compartmentalized knowledge. Sparse upcycling reaches better MoEs at about 50% of the dense sunk cost by copying a dense MLP into experts, which is duplication-divergence in LLMs. BTX and Lifelong-MoE grow experts over time. The ML evidence is at large scale (vision, LLMs); the biological evidence is comparative and partly hypothetical.
candidates.risks: Module size and port count are hand-chosen, which is hard-coding the user dislikes; mitigate by letting modules be lineages from candidate A. It may drift into conventional MoE engineering. Frozen modules can block adaptation (the stability-plasticity trade-off). The ladder must actually reward reuse: dot to mouse is close, text is far. Duplicates may stay redundant without an energy or connection cost to force divergence.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: modules are 16-unit GRU/LIF blocks in torch; task 1 is dot-chase with 1-2 modules. Week 2: task 2, 'mouse cursor' (the target follows smooth human-like trajectories with acceleration and turns, so prediction pays). Compare duplicate-trained-organs against fresh modules and against fine-tuning one large module. Week 3: task 3, a toy text stream (symbols map to directions, or next-character prediction steering the body) to test reuse at a larger distance. Compute: one GPU, 1-3 days. Success on task 2: duplicated-organ bodies reach the from-scratch final score with at least 3x fewer samples, keep at least 95% of their task-1 score, and knockouts show both copies used (divergence, not redundancy).
candidates.relaxes: Relaxes the clock partially (lockstep inside modules, asynchronous between them). Cells are replaced as the top-level unit, though they can survive inside modules. One continuous life becomes optional (a ladder can run within one long life or across many). Spikes are optional. It is the closest match to the user's planned ladder (dot, mouse, text) and to multi-core hardware, and the most direct use of how current ML scales (MoE, upcycling).

candidates.unit: Neurons sit at 3D positions on a substrate; the hex-prism lattice can be the substrate. Each neuron is an LIF or rate unit. The genome is a CPPN (NEAT-evolved, about 10-50 nodes with sin/gauss/sigmoid/abs activations), plus optionally the GRN. It is queried as f(p_i, p_j, delta_p, gene states at i and j) and returns (weight, delay, plasticity coefficients A, B, C, D, eta, express?). ES-HyperNEAT's quadtree places hidden neurons where the CPPN pattern carries information, so density is evolved, not set by hand.
candidates.communication: Any pair within a radius (or any pair) may connect, as the CPPN decides, so circuits are multidirectional and recurrent. Messages are spikes or rates. Direction comes free: weight sign as a function of delta_z is exactly the 'excite going up, inhibit coming down' rule the pilot evolved through costly chemistry.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: NEAT on the CPPN (complexification, speciation), or ES on a fixed-size CPPN on GPU. Inner loop: weights are plastic under the CPPN-given local rule (adaptive HyperNEAT; Najarro & Risi style), modulated by a reward neuromodulator that diffuses locally.
candidates.growth: Growth means more resolution or more extent: re-query the CPPN at more positions. A new neuron's weights blend the genetic prior (the CPPN) with learned weights interpolated from nearby older neurons, an 'upsampling' of the learned weight field, and it enters with a fade-in gain. Within one life, density can increase over time, with daughters placed by the GRN and wired by the CPPN. Evolve at small size (cheap, low noise), then deploy and keep evolving at larger size.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary recurrent circuits with geometric regularity. Irregular one-off circuits are harder to express, because CPPN encodings are biased toward regularity.
candidates.hardware: CPPN queries are one big batched MLP over neuron pairs (N^2, or N x k neighbours), trivial on a GPU. The runtime network is a sparse or dense matmul. On chip, weights can be generated on the fly from positions instead of stored, which saves memory, and plasticity stays local.
candidates.evidence: HyperNEAT and ES-HyperNEAT evolve large geometric networks; the ES-HyperNEAT abstract reports neural topography and geometric regularity on maze-navigation and modular-retina tasks. I recall that HyperNEAT 2009 showed a visual-discrimination network evolved at low substrate resolution working at higher resolution without further evolution, but I could not open the paper to confirm it, so treat that as unverified. Najarro & Risi 2020 evolved rules for about 450k plastic synapses that self-organize from random weights within a life. HyperNCA and NDP are the neural-CA descendants of this line.
candidates.risks: CPPNs favour regular patterns, so fine irregular circuits may be out of reach. Growth by upsampling preserves function only if the learned computation is smooth in space. NEAT on CPPNs can stagnate. It adds a second genome beside the GRN and moves part of the cell-level decision-making into a global-looking function of geometry. Each query is still local (it uses only the two positions and their genes), but it is less emergent than A.
candidates.prototype: Week 1: a CPPN (an ES-optimised MLP of fixed size, simpler than NEAT for a first test) producing weights and plasticity on a 64-cell 3-plane lattice in the batched dot-chase world. Week 2: evolve at N = 64 for about 200 generations, then regrow at N = 256 and N = 1024 and test zero-shot. Week 3: add fade-in growth during one life. Compute: one GPU, about 2 days. Success: zero-shot F at 4x the size is at least 90% of the small body's F, against under 50% for a direct-encoded network enlarged by nearest-neighbour copying.
candidates.relaxes: Partly replaces GRN-driven development with a geometric genome, so less cell-level emergence. Relaxes the clock in training (GPU lockstep). Keeps local plasticity, one life and arbitrary recurrence. Worth testing because it is the cleanest 'learn small, deploy big' mechanism, and its per-edge directional rule removes the morphogen-chemistry tax the pilot found.

explored.cross_cutting:
1) Make every structural mutation neutral at birth, and measure it. Today each child is about 0.19 F worse than its parent. Add a standard readout, the 'birth deficit' (child F minus parent F at birth, with CRN), and prefer operators that make it about 0. You can do this in the current C kernel now. The GRN update is s_k = sigma(b_k + sum_j W[k][j] x_j), g_k += lam_k (s_k - g_k) (LIF_ABI.md section 7, step 4). So a function-preserving gene duplication of k into a free slot k' is: copy row k (b, W[k][:], lam, Q) to k'; set W[j][k] = W[j][k'] = W[j][k]/2 for every row j; start g_k' = g_k; and halve the phenotype readout from k across both copies if it is linear in g. Both copies then stay identical, and the dynamics stay bitwise identical because halving is exact in binary floating point, until a later mutation hits one copy. That makes duplication (currently off, with the gene count stuck at 8) a free, neutral source of new genes: Ohno's route, and Force et al.'s DDC. The same principle covers neurons (Net2Net split), edges (zero init, GradMax direction), nodes (NEAT add-node) and modules (copy with outputs halved). This is my cheapest recommendation: days of work, no paradigm change.
2) Fade in when exactness is impossible (lattice placement, spike thresholds). New structure gets an output gain that ramps from 0 to 1 under local or GRN control: masked structural growth (Yao et al. 2024), GAN fade-in (Karras et al. 2018), adult-born neurons.
3) Grow where the learning signal says so. Splitting-matrix sign (Liu et al. 2019), GradMax gradient norms, the SENN natural expansion score and NORTH orthogonality are all computed from a unit's own activity and error signal. Feed one of them to the GRN as an input rather than hard-coding 'divide when X', so growth stays emergent but informed.
4) Lamarckian and Baldwinian mixtures. Inherit slow learned weights and reset fast ones, or inherit with some probability. Hinton & Nowlan (1987, Complex Systems 1(3), https://www.complex-systems.com/abstracts/v01_i03_a06/) showed that learning smooths the landscape evolution searches; that matters here, where per-life reliability is 0.026.
5) Protect new structure with speciation. The pilot collapses to one lineage by generation 2-119. NEAT species, compared by historical markings, protect neutral new structure for the generations it needs before it pays, and markings let differently grown bodies cross over.
6) Use GPUs now and stay clockless where it counts. Train in lockstep with randomized update masks, jittered delays and dt sweeps (Growing NCA; DiffLogic CA), then certify winners in the existing exact event-driven kernel. Behaviour that survives is clock-independent, which keeps the long-run asynchronous-hardware target open.
7) Choose hardware-native units from the start. Fixed point is already shown fitness-neutral. A shared cell program is one datapath replicated per tile. Differentiable logic-gate cells (Petersen et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08277; DiffLogic CA 2025) are trained by gradient, then become pure gates for FPGA/ASIC.
8) Beat Poisson noise with breadth. On GPU, 64-256 CRN lives per genome cost little and cut the standard error 8-16x, so selection can finally see differences of about 0.2 F.
9) Make 'learn small, then expand' an explicit protocol. Evolve tiny bodies first (cheap and nearly exact under CRN). Expand only lineages that have plateaued, using a neutral growth operator, and keep a protected copy (Progressive nets / PathNet) when the task changes, so the ladder (dot, mouse, text) accumulates organs instead of overwriting them.
Suggested order: item 1 in the current kernel (days); then A (closest to the project, GPU-native); B as the best-case ML reference at equal GPU-time; C when moving to the mouse and text tasks; D if A's bodies need to be rescaled to larger sizes.

explored.angle:
Hardware-native and massively parallel evolution and learning. The question here is which way of writing "cells + local messages + growth" suits GPUs now and FPGAs/ASICs later, and how much throughput it gains over 0.1 CPU-s per life.

Two baseline numbers frame everything:
- Today a life costs about $2-5e-7 on a rented spot core (c7a.48xlarge at $3.40/h over 192 cores; 0.1 CPU-s per life on the loaded laptop, a server core is perhaps 2-2.6x faster). So dollars are not the bottleneck.
- What limits the project is search efficiency: per-life reliability is 0.026, each child is about 0.19 F worse than its parent, and runs collapse to one lineage. Hardware therefore pays only where it buys one of three things:
  (a) 10-100x more lives per generation, so noise can be averaged and populations can be large or diverse;
  (b) gradients, i.e. dense credit assignment;
  (c) an evolved artefact that is already a circuit.

I compared three paradigms on these terms and ran two light stand-in benchmarks on the laptop (Ultra 7 255U, one core). Sources are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-jgon-project-ml-cell-dev/aefb0c66-3af5-49c4-936c-154d6434706c/scratchpad/alt/hardware/ (bitslice.c, bitslice2.c, bitslice3.c with gen.py, nca_bench.py).

1. **Bit-sliced logic tissue** (candidate 1, the most hardware-native). Measured: 2.6-7.6 ms per life, i.e. 13-40x below today's kernel per CPU core, before world and growth bookkeeping are added.
2. **Tensor spiking tissue with ES at scale and evolved plasticity** (candidate 2, the smallest departure). Gains are modest per dollar (the repo's own estimate is 2-9x). Its first week also measures the open dt question and runs a gradient "oracle" that tells whether the routing gap is a search problem or a substrate problem.
3. **Vector-message NCA-style tissue trained by gradients inside an evolutionary outer loop** (candidate 3, the most mainstream ML). Measured on CPU: 0.31-0.67 s per life, 3-7x slower than today. On a GPU it is estimated at roughly cost parity to 4x cheaper per life, but each cell does 10-40x more arithmetic and gradients become available.

candidates.communication:
Value-less bits, as today:
- 1 bit per channel per face per step.
- Delay lines of 1-3 steps, with a random per-message choice of length, imitate delay jitter.
- Each step, a per-site random update mask (p about 0.5) decides which cells update, so behaviour cannot rely on lockstep order. This is the asynchronous-CA approximation used by DiffLogic CA and Growing NCA.

Direction. Two options:
- **Fixed face index.** The circuit sees which face each bit came from. This fixes the up/down versus in-plane asymmetry without chemistry, but a fixed in-plane face index acts like a hard-coded compass.
- **Polarity-relative faces (closer to the minimal-hardcoding preference).** In-plane faces are presented rotated relative to a learned polarity state of the cell, or pooled as counts and ORs, as in Isotropic NCA.
candidates.learning:
**Outer loop:**
- CGP-style mutation of gate types and wiring, with inactive genes giving neutral drift. CGP's neutral drift also addresses the drift the pilot lost through 'parents win ties'.
- A (mu+lambda) GA or MAP-Elites archive.
- Fitness averaged over the 64-256 bit-sliced lives of each genome. The bit-slicing structurally forces many common-random-number lives per genome, which is exactly what the Poisson noise needs.

**Optional gradient phase** (memetic):
1. Relax the gates as in DiffLogic: each gate is a softmax over the 16 two-input functions.
2. Train the cell circuit by BPTT on small tissues against a differentiable expected-capture surrogate, or distil it from probe traces of evolved bodies.
3. Discretise, then evolve.

**Inner loop (within life):** only through state bits. Example: a per-face enable bit that a learned local rule sets or clears is binary plasticity. There is no float learning inside the life.
candidates.growth:
**Within a life:**
- Divide bits claim an empty neighbour. Simultaneous claims are resolved locally by random priority bits, with no order dependence.
- The daughter copies the mother's state bits, so anything learned in life (latch, gain or enable bits) spreads as the tissue grows.

**The genome:**
- New gates enter as pass-throughs (identity truth table, the residual initialisation of Petersen 2024) or as inactive CGP nodes. Growth is therefore function-preserving.
- A gate budget raised by stages gives 'learn small, then expand'.

Because all cells share one netlist, a rule found in a 20-cell tissue runs unchanged in a 300-cell one. To make it robust to size, evolve it across a distribution of n_max and world sizes.
candidates.circuitry: Any recurrent, multidirectional circuit among cells via face bits. Each step's netlist is feedforward, and the state bits make the cell recurrent. Inhibition, latches and feedback are just gates. Long-range circuits need relay cells or axon slots (see cross-cutting).
candidates.hardware:
**CPU, measured** (stand-in: random netlist, 300 active sites, 4,096 steps, 64 circuit inputs; no world, no hex routing, no growth bookkeeping):
- interpreted netlist: 7.6 ms per life;
- straight-line compiled netlist: 4.2 ms per life;
- compiled with AVX2 over 256 lives: 2.6 ms per life (2.4e11 gate-evals/s).

That is 13-40x below today's 0.1 CPU-s per life, before adding the world per lane (cheap: one dot per life) and growth. Per rented core that would be about $1-3e-8 per life [E].

**GPU** [E, not measured]:
- Bitwise ops on 32-bit lanes; NVIDIA's lop3 instruction evaluates any 3-input boolean function in one op (not re-verified here).
- Assuming about 1.7e13 int32 ops/s on an H100 and 32 lanes per op: about 5e14 gate-evals/s theoretical.
- That is about 10^5 lives/s at this cell size at 10-20% efficiency, plausibly 10-100x cheaper per life than today's kernel.

**FPGA** [E, unverified]:
- Gates pack several to a LUT6.
- A programmable cell (truth tables in registers, input muxes) of about 500 gates is maybe 1-3k LUTs, so on the order of hundreds of cells per VU47P at 200-400 MHz.
- One 4,096-step life would take 10-20 µs if the world also lives in fabric.
- Compare HARDWARE_PATH's integer-GRN FPGA: 0.2-1.2 of a CPU box.

**ASIC:** a tile is a few thousand gates plus a configuration register. That is far smaller than the GRN tile, where the 13.5 kbit genome is about 9x a cell's own state.
candidates.evidence:
Proven:
- DLGN inference beyond 1M MNIST images/s per CPU core (2022).
- 61M-gate CIFAR-10 networks at 86.29% (2024).
- Logic CA learn Game of Life (336 gates) and morphogenesis (lizard, 577 gates), and train under asynchronous updates with improved robustness (2025).
- LUT networks deploy on FPGAs at nanosecond latency (LogicNets 2020, DWN 2024).
- CGP has evolved digital circuits since 1997-2000.

Not shown anywhere (to my knowledge, without a search to confirm):
- a logic CA steering a body in closed loop;
- one learning within a life;
- one evolved, rather than gradient-trained, on a closed-loop task;
- relaxed training over thousands of recurrent steps.
candidates.risks:
1. **Relaxed-to-discrete gap and vanishing gradients** over long horizons. DiffLogic CA trained short rollouts.
2. **Graded integration costs gates.** Counters cost many gates, which could push evolution toward large circuits or brittle spike timing.
3. **Mutational fragility.** Random gate edits can be catastrophic. Neutral drift and inactive genes help, but CGP is slow on large circuits.
4. **Bit-slicing needs one genome per word.** Populations become many words of 64-256 lives each, fine for noise but wasteful when screening thousands of founders cheaply.
5. **Lost features.** The analog GRN dynamics (s2's slow in-life gain drift) must be re-evolved as state bits.
6. **Clock and timing.** Step-synchronous with random masks, so behaviour could still exploit step granularity unless checked under varied masks and delays.
7. **Configurable hardware costs area.** Changing a genome on an FPGA means rewriting truth-table registers, not resynthesising, which costs area.
candidates.relaxes:
**Relaxed:**
- The clock. Steps with random update masks and jittered delays replace exact event times.
- The continuous membrane and GRN, which become bits and counters.

**Kept:** spikes as bits, one continuous life, growth, death, local rules and a shared genome.

**Why it might be worth it:** it is the only paradigm where the evolved artefact is the hardware itself (a netlist), it is the cheapest per life on a CPU today, and it puts the 'native on hardware' goal in reach without a separate integer ABI port.

Replace the (32+224) GA with large-population ES and QD that averages noisy lives instead of ranking them. Give cells per-face plastic weights driven by a genome-set eligibility-times-neuromodulator rule, so local improvements are learned within a life and copied to daughters. candidates.unit:
Today's cell (LIF membrane, 2 channels, GRN with 8-16 genes, morphogens), plus:
- per-face, per-channel signed weights w[f,c] (the X1 face-weight proposal, still awaiting approval);
- an eligibility trace e[f,c] per weight.

GRN outputs set the plasticity gain, sign and decay as gene expression, so evolution decides which cells and planes learn and when. Development stays evolutionary and discrete.

Because every cell of a life shares one genome, the GRN tick for the whole tissue is one small dense GEMM, n_cells x (inputs+16) times a fixed matrix, which suits tensor cores. Membrane and spike updates are elementwise.
candidates.communication:
- **Spikes:** 1 bit per channel per face per step through circular delay buffers, with per-message jitter of 1-2 steps.
- **Clock:** dt = 1/16-1/4, and each cell has its own random tick phase.
- **Neuromodulator:** a diffusing chemical in the existing morphogen machinery. It is released locally by cells that sense the consequences of their acts (capture or miss at the hotspot, contact). It is not a global broadcast, which keeps the rule local.
candidates.learning:
**Outer loop:**
- OpenES, SNES or CMA-ES (evosax or EvoTorch).
- 2k-20k antithetic perturbation pairs per generation.
- Each pair shares the same life seeds (common random numbers), and fitness is rank-shaped.
- The genome is about 875 floats, small for ES. ES turns many low-reliability lives into one gradient estimate instead of trying to rank individuals.
- Discrete structure (gene duplication, division geometry) can stay with a GA or MAP-Elites, giving a hybrid.

**Inner loop:** a three-factor rule dw = eta(genes) * e * m, plus homeostatic decay. This is e-prop-like, with symbolic variants searchable as in Jordan et al.

**Diagnostic oracle (not part of the organism):** after development, freeze the body and train its face weights and thresholds by surrogate-gradient BPTT on the expected-capture objective. Alternatively, run EventProp, the exact adjoint at spike times, on the event-driven kernel itself. This asks whether this substrate can express routing that beats the reflex.
candidates.growth:
**Within a life:**
- Same division, claim and death laws as now, on a padded lattice whose capacity is the existing n_max guard.
- Births are masked writes; simultaneous claims are resolved by random keys (local, order-free).
- Daughters inherit the mother's learned weights and traces. This is cell-level inheritance within one life, so a local improvement learned while the tissue is small is replicated as it grows (a biological analogue is epigenetic inheritance).

**Genome growth:** gene duplication with the copy's outputs zero-initialised, which is function-preserving and already in the code but turned off. Evolution can also be run with a size curriculum: n_max and world size grow over generations.
candidates.circuitry: Per-face per-channel signed plastic weights express any directed relation between neighbours (for example, excite going up and inhibit coming down), with no morphogen hack. Feedback and recurrence are native. Long-range connections need relays or axon slots (cross-cutting).
candidates.hardware:
**GPU now** (the repo's own estimates in docs/HARDWARE_PATH.md):
- H100 about 4.4 CPU boxes per wall-hour at dt 0.1, about 2.2-5.6x cheaper per unit of work.
- L4 about 9x cheaper.
- At dt 1/16-1/64: 0.05-17x.
- Effort 6-14 pw.

So per life this is modest. The win is statistical: 10-100x more lives per generation, enough for ES populations of 10^4 with common random numbers.

**Later:**
- LIF plus online eligibility-trace learning already exists in silicon (ReckOn).
- Fixed point is fitness-neutral here [M, -0.012 ± 0.020 F].
- EGGROLL trains integer-only recurrent models by ES, so the integer ABI can be the evolved object itself.
- Loihi-class chips and the asynchronous tile chip of HARDWARE_PATH both fit. Plasticity adds one weight and one trace per face-channel, about 16 x 2 x 12-16 bits per cell.
candidates.evidence:
- **ES at scale:** Salimans 2017 (>1,000 workers), EGGROLL 2025 (~100x faster at large populations; integer-only models), Qiu 2025 (full-parameter ES on billion-parameter LLMs).
- **Evolved plasticity:** fast adaptation (Najarro & Risi 2020: <100 steps after damage); Jordan et al. 2021 recovered and discovered spiking plasticity rules.
- **SNN training:** e-prop approximates BPTT online; EventProp gives exact event-based gradients, 3x faster and 4x leaner than surrogates in GeNN.
- **In-repo:** s2 already adapts its gain within life over tens to about 100 units, so in-life adaptation is useful in this world. Faster conduction helps every body (+0.14 to +1.70).
candidates.risks:
1. **Clock artefacts.** At dt 1/16, 6-10% of a cell's arrivals coincide with another input [M, repo]; which dt preserves behaviour is unmeasured.
2. **Port cost.** The full port is 6-14 pw.
3. **ES on development.** Division events make the landscape discontinuous, so ES gradient estimates for developmental genes may be poor (hence the hybrid).
4. **Plasticity may go unused,** like apoptosis, unless the world changes within a life. It needs within-life variety (shifted worlds, decoys).
5. **Neuromodulator credit assignment is slow:** about 19 captures per 1,024-unit life give few reward events.
6. **Oracle caveat.** The gradient oracle's smoothed objective must be the expectation of the real score, not a proxy; the design review rejected distance-based shaping because it breeds parking.
candidates.prototype:
3 weeks, on the laptop CPU plus one rented L4 or RTX 4090 for a few days (under $100).

**Week 1.** Export the post-development phenotype of the reflex, the router, s2, s4, s5 and s6 from the probe toolkit (positions, effective per-face weights, thresholds). Re-run it as a time-stepped torch model with the world in torch. Run 1,024 paired lives at dt 1/4, 1/16 and 1/64 against the exact kernel. This is the first measurement of which dt leaves F unchanged, an open question in HARDWARE_PATH.

**Week 2.** Gradient oracle: surrogate-gradient training of face weights and thresholds on the frozen s5 and s6 bodies. In parallel, run antithetic ES with common random numbers (population 2k) on the same parameters, and ES on the full genome with the current CPU kernel (no GPU needed) at equal lives against the GA.

**Week 3.** Add a three-factor rule with 6-10 evolved coefficients and a local neuromodulator. Test within-life learning in the four shifted worlds.

**Success:**
- (a) A dt with |dF| < 0.1 for all six bodies, or a documented dependence.
- (b) Gradient-tuned s5/s6 bodies beat +8.69: then the routing gap is a search problem, so prioritise ES and plasticity. If they cannot, the substrate or protocol is the limit, so move to candidates 1 and 3.
- (c) Capture retention in shifted worlds rises from 0.47-0.53 to 0.6 or more with plasticity on.
- (d) ES beats the GA at equal lives on at least 2 of 3 seeds.

- Gradients appear only as an offline diagnostic.

**Kept:** spikes, LIF, GRN, morphogens, one continuous life, growth and death.

**Why it might be worth it:** it is the cheapest way to learn whether the bottleneck is the search (noise, small populations) or the substrate. It also adds within-life learning that grows with the tissue, which is the user's 'learn small, expand on growth' in its most literal form.

candidates.unit:
**State:** a vector of 16-32 channels, including an alive/maturity channel and gene-like hidden channels.

**Rule:** one shared rule (the genome is the network weights, about 2-10k parameters, against 875 today). Inputs: own state, the 8 face messages, local world inputs, a noise channel. Outputs: a state delta, one outgoing message per face, divide and die logits with direction, act outputs (twitch, tap).

**Hardware path:** an optional straight-through binary 'spike' output channel, plus int8 quantisation-aware training.
candidates.communication:
- **Messages:** real-valued vectors of 4-8 dimensions per face, delayed 1-2 steps at random.
- **Asynchrony:** a stochastic update mask (p about 0.5), as in Growing NCA.
- **Direction:** the cell knows which face a message came from, either through a face embedding, or (isotropic option) faces rotated into the cell's own learned polarity frame, as in Isotropic NCA.
- **Representation:** an occupied-cell list with a padded neighbour index table [N_max, K] and gathers. This runs the same code on lattices and on arbitrary grown graphs, and avoids wasting compute on empty sites; only about 20-25% of sites hold cells today.
candidates.learning:
**Inner loop (training the shared rule):** truncated, rematerialised BPTT through development and behaviour on a differentiable expected-capture objective. The BODY-1 world is a dot with targets, simple enough to write differentiably in JAX or torch. The arm against it is OpenES (evosax) with antithetic common random numbers, and a combined arm uses gradient warm-start then ES.

**Within-life learning:** optional fast weights or per-face state, in the VSML style.

**Outer loop:** PBT, QD or evolution over rule width and depth, message width, developmental hyperparameters, curriculum schedule and world niches. Evolution handles the discrete choices and keeps diversity; gradients do the fine local tuning that evolution does slowly, where today each child is about 0.19 F worse than its parent.
candidates.growth:
**Tissue:** a soft alive channel (as in NCA) plus discrete division claims with random-priority conflict resolution.

**Curriculum:** raise n_max from 16 to 64 to 256, and world size and target speed with it.

**Network:** function-preserving widening. Net2Net copies hidden units; new message channels and genes start with zero output weights.

**Learn small, expand later:** the rule is shared and local, so a rule learned at 16 cells already runs at 256. Training over a size distribution keeps it valid; s2's outward relay flips from costly to useful at about 60-75 cells, which shows why that matters.

To stay closest to 'evolutionary growth', each curriculum stage can be a PBT generation that copies the best rule and widens it.
candidates.circuitry:
Fully multidirectional and recurrent through face messages.

With the gather representation, cells can grow long-range edges (axon slots, as in NDP and LNDP graph growth), so circuits are not limited to lattice adjacency. This matters here: the routing gap was 'earnings per cell', and relaying across a lattice costs cells.
candidates.hardware:
**CPU, measured** (stand-in, one laptop core, torch: 300 cells, 4,096 steps, a batch of 256 lives sharing one genome):
- small rule (16 channels, 4-dim messages, 32 hidden): 0.31 s per life, 3.8 GMAC per life;
- larger rule (32 channels, 8-dim messages, 64 hidden): 0.67 s per life, 15 GMAC per life.
That is 3-7x slower than today's kernel on a CPU.

**GPU** [E, not measured]: about 10^3-10^4 lives/s per H100 if the whole life is fused (the state of 300 cells fits in on-chip shared memory). At an assumed $2-3/h that is roughly cost parity to 4x cheaper per life than today, while each cell does 10-40x the arithmetic of a GRN tick, and gradients are available. CAX reports up to 2,000x speed-ups for CA in JAX against conventional implementations.

**FPGA and ASIC:** the weakest of the three candidates. An int8 MLP cell needs thousands of MACs per update, so the hardware would be time-multiplexed MAC arrays rather than a tile per cell. Distilling the trained rule into candidate 1's logic circuit is a possible path.
candidates.evidence:
- **Growth and repair:** NCA grow, keep and repair 2D patterns with about 8k parameters under random update masks, and grow 3D structures and functional machines; evolved NCA regrow soft-robot bodies.
- **Consensus:** local messages reach global consensus (self-classifying MNIST).
- **Grown controllers:** HyperNCA, NDP and LNDP grow controllers for small RL tasks. LNDP adds activity- and reward-dependent structural plasticity.
- **Message-passing control:** shared modules with bidirectional messages control and generalise across morphologies (SMP; Pathak 2019).
- **Learned learning:** VSML shows shared tiny recurrent units with forward and backward messages can meta-learn a learning algorithm.
- **Gap:** no NCA has done closed-loop body control with sensor-driven targets at this project's noise level, and gradient training through discrete growth is only partly solved, via soft alive masks.
candidates.risks:
1. **Over-powerful messages.** High-bandwidth messages may let the tissue 'cheat' by doing global computation in a few cells.
2. **Opacity.** An MLP cell is harder to dissect than the GRN, although lesion probes still work.
3. **Unstable rollouts.** Gradient training of NCA is known to be unstable over long rollouts and needs pools and damage training. BPTT over a 1,024-unit life needs truncation, which biases credit assignment toward short timescales.
4. **Proxy breeding.** A differentiable surrogate must be the expectation of the real score; a distance-shaped proxy breeds parking, as the design review found.
5. **Distance from the long-term goal.** It moves furthest from spikes and native hardware.
6. **Rental required.** It needs rented GPUs (none locally) and a new JAX or torch simulator; house style is torch, and the GPU-evolution ecosystem is mostly JAX.
candidates.relaxes:
**Relaxed:**
- Spikes, which become vector messages (a binary straight-through channel can bring them back).
- The clock, which becomes steps with random masks.
- GRN interpretability.
- 'Evolution only': gradients become the main inner optimiser.

**Kept:** one continuous life (truncated BPTT needs no resets), local shared rules, growth and death.

**Why it might be worth it:** it is where current ML tooling, tensor cores and the differentiable world are strongest. It is also the fastest way to find out what a local, growing, message-passing tissue can do on this task when credit assignment is not the bottleneck. Its rules can then be distilled into candidates 1 or 2.

explored.cross_cutting:
1. **Change the outer loop before changing the hardware.** The genome is only about 875 floats, and per-life reliability is 0.026.
   - Antithetic ES (OpenES, SNES or CMA-ES), where each pair shares life seeds (common random numbers), turns many noisy lives into one gradient estimate. Truncation selection instead tries to rank individuals that cannot be told apart.
   - This runs on today's exact CPU kernel, with no model change. Test it against the GA at equal lives, together with random tie-breaking.
   - For later, larger rules, EGGROLL-style low-rank perturbations keep ES near inference throughput.

2. **Quality-diversity against single-lineage collapse.** Runs collapse by generation 2-119.
   - Use a MAP-Elites archive (Mouret & Clune 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.04909, opened; QDax, Chalumeau et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03665, opened).
   - Descriptors from the mechanisms the probes already measure: lateral share of F, cells at t=64, channel use, final size, world niche.
   - Leniabreeder (Faldor & Cully 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04235, opened) is a working example of QD on a CA in JAX.

3. **Learn small, expand on growth, at three levels:**
   - (a) **Shared local rules are size-agnostic.** Train and evolve over a distribution of n_max and world sizes, then raise both on a schedule, as a curriculum inside evolution.
   - (b) **Function-preserving genome growth.**
     - Net2Net widening (Chen et al. 2016).
     - Zero-output gene duplication (already in code, turned off).
     - Pass-through gates (DiffLogic residual initialisation).
     - Splitting one cell type into two copies that then diverge, the analogue of sparse upcycling (Komatsuzaki et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05055, opened: upcycled models beat dense ones at about 50% of the sunk cost).
   - (c) **Cell-level inheritance.** Daughters copy the mother's learned weights, traces or state bits, so a local trick learned while the tissue is small replicates as it grows within one life.

4. **A 'clockless gate' instead of a clockless simulator.** Train fast in lockstep steps, but with random per-cell update masks and jittered delays, and keep only rules whose F stays within tolerance when re-scored in the exact event-driven kernel or the integer ABI's window scheduler. This keeps the no-lockstep preference as a test, which is cheaper than making it a simulator constraint.
   - Separately, EventProp (Wunderlich & Pehle 2021) could give exact, clockless gradients of synaptic parameters directly on the existing event-driven kernel. Development would stay evolutionary.

5. **Gradients as a diagnostic, even with an evolution-only philosophy.** Train frozen grown bodies by surrogate gradients or EventProp to find the substrate's ceiling.
   - If no weight setting on s5's 122 cells beats the reflex, more search will not help; change the protocol (face weights, axons, richer messages).
   - If one does, the problem is search, so use ES, larger populations, plasticity and QD.

6. **Axon slots for truly arbitrary circuitry.** Each cell gets K long-range edge slots, each holding a target and a delay.
   - They are grown by a growth-cone walk along a morphogen gradient and pruned by activity.
   - Storage is padded index tables: gathers on a GPU, address-event packets on a network-on-chip on an FPGA or ASIC (SpiNNaker-style).
   - This addresses the 'earnings per cell' gap, where relaying across a lattice costs cells.

7. **GPU engineering facts that decide the gains:**
   - Batch many lives of one genome, which suits both common random numbers and bit-slicing.
   - Store occupied cells as lists with a neighbour table rather than a dense lattice; only about 20-25% of sites are occupied.
   - Fuse a whole life into one kernel: 300 cells x 32 channels fits in on-chip shared memory. Start with vmap+scan (JAX) or torch.func, then move to Pallas, Triton or CUDA.
   - The GPU-evolution ecosystem is JAX (evosax, EvoJAX by Tang, Tian & Ha 2022 at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05008, opened: 'minutes on a single accelerator, compared to hours or days on CPUs'; QDax; CAX; Brax/MJX; Kinetix/Jax2D). The torch-native options are EvoTorch and torch.func, and TensorNEAT (Wang et al. 2024, https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01817, opened: up to 500x over NEAT-Python by padding variable topologies into tensors) shows growing topologies can be tensorised.
   - There is no GPU on this laptop, so every GPU number here is an estimate. The H100 integer throughput and the $2-3/h price are assumptions I did not verify.

8. **Integer and bit precision throughout.** Fixed point is fitness-neutral here [M]. Evolution does not need differentiability, so int8 or bit tissues can be evolved directly; EGGROLL even pretrains integer-only recurrent models by ES. The evolved object is then already the hardware reference, which serves the ABI-4 integer-twin plan.

9. **Suggested order:**
   1. ES with common random numbers on the current kernel (days, no new hardware).
   2. Candidate 2, weeks 1-2: the dt-equivalence measurement and the gradient oracle, which together say search or substrate.
   3. Candidate 1's CPU bit-sliced logic tissue: no GPU needed, the largest measured per-core gain (13-40x in a stand-in benchmark) and the most direct path to native hardware.
   4. Candidate 3 on a rented GPU, only if the oracle says the spike protocol itself is the limit.

explored.angle: Current ML frontier directions, used to change how cell-dev searches rather than to replace its goal. Four strands: (a) LLM-driven program evolution (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, ELM, ShinkaEvolve/OpenEvolve; AutoML-Zero as the LLM-free control); (b) meta-learned shared local rules that learn in context (VSML, GPICL, NCA, NDP/LNDP, Continuous Thought Machines), searched with GPU evolution strategies (evosax, EvoJAX, EGGROLL); (c) open-ended co-generation of worlds and solvers with foundation-model curators (POET, Enhanced POET, OMNI, OMNI-EPIC, ASAL, Kinetix, Darwin Godel Machine); (d) local world models: predictive or self-supervised learning inside each cell, with evolution acting on development (Greedy InfoMax, predictive coding, e-prop, Hinton & Nowlan's Baldwin effect). Each candidate below is matched to the pilot's measured bottlenecks: selection noise (per-life SD 2.0-2.5 F, so small mutations cannot be seen), small random mutations (children about 0.19 F worse than parents), no direct directional synapse primitive, collapse to one lineage, inert hidden planes in a reactive world, and an event-driven kernel that does not fit GPUs. Verification notes: web search was exhausted this session, so every citation was checked by fetching its arXiv, journal or Europe PMC page directly. The FunSearch first author was confirmed through Europe PMC (Romera-Paredes; Fawzi is the last author). e-prop and Oh et al. 2025 were confirmed from Europe PMC metadata only. EGGROLL was seen only in an arXiv listing. Two arXiv API queries found no paper that uses an LLM to evolve NCA, developmental or plasticity rules for a growing multicellular tissue. Not finding one does not show none exists, but it suggests candidate 1 would be new work.

candidates.unit: The same site and cell as ABI 3. The genome becomes (program text, constant vector). The program is a restricted integer C subset, Q10 or finer to respect the integer-ABI precision traps. It fills the bodies of handlers the kernel already has: on_tick (which today runs TICK steps 3-8: gene update, phenotype decode, death draw, division placement), on_arrival(face d, channel c), on_receptor, and on_birth(inherited registers). State is a fixed register file, for example 16 int16 'genes' plus per-face 8x2 int8 in and out weights and counters. The GRN stays available as one callable primitive (grn_step), so the first program is exactly today's GRN mode, and 'program mode' (ABI 4.5/7.5) already shows the kernel can host a non-GRN cell. Observables are whitelisted to exactly what the GRN sees today (own genes, morphogen levels, firing and receptor traces, n_view, the plane cues, the face of an arrival). A linter rejects any other identifier, any unbounded loop and any float, so the LLM cannot introduce global information or designed roles beyond what a cell could sense.
candidates.communication: Unchanged and enforced by the harness, not by the evolved code: value-less spikes on 2 channels, morphogen packets, every effect delayed by at least d_min, event-driven and clockless, with no reading of a neighbour's state. One new expressive freedom: the handler knows which face an arrival came through and may weight or gate it. Direction-specific synapses, the review's top lever, become expressible directly without being hard-coded, so evolution can find them without morphogen chemistry, or ignore them. Instructions executed per event are charged as energy, like firing and living, so cheap programs win and the result stays sized for a hardware cell.
candidates.learning: Outer loop, two timescales. (1) Structure: an LLM proposes diffs to a parent program, or merges two parents (FunSearch-style best-shot prompting with k=2), inside 4-8 islands with ring migration and a MAP-Elites grid (descriptors: cells at T/2, lateral share from lateral_off, program length). The prompt carries the parent's code, the world spec (ABI 9.7) and an automatic probe.py report: knockout table, lineage of act cells, size curve, lateral_off and hidden_off deltas. This is Eureka/ReEvo-style reflection, and cell-dev's probe tooling is an unusual asset here. (2) Constants: short bursts of the existing (32+224) GA or CMA-ES on the constant vector for structures that pass the cascade. Evaluation is a cascade under common random numbers: 16, then 64, then 256 lives. Inner loop (within life): whatever the program implements. Counters, coincidence-gated weight changes and homeostatic set points are all writable, so within-life plasticity stops being limited to gene-expression drift. Control arm: the same loop with the LLM replaced by AutoML-Zero-style random instruction insert, delete and randomize, which measures what the LLM prior adds.
candidates.growth: Development is part of the program (claim, placement, death, inherited registers), as in today's GRN. Learning small and expanding later works as a staged curriculum over body cap and field size. The stage-k prompt includes the stage-(k-1) elite. A child must first pass a regression gate (at least 90% of its parent's F on the parent's world) before it is scored on the bigger world, so algorithms found at small size are kept as reusable functions and then extended. Code-level gene duplication (copy a handler branch for a new internal state, then specialise) is an explicit mutation prompt. At introduction it preserves function, in the same sense as Net2Net.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary and multidirectional. The program decides per face what to send and how to weigh what arrives, so feedforward, lateral, feedback and recurrent loops are all expressible on the lattice. A capped radius gene (the user's 2026-10-07 idea) can be added as one more whitelisted action, a relay to the k-hop neighbourhood with delay growing with distance, without breaking locality.
candidates.hardware: Evaluation stays on the existing CPU C kernel, which the hardware study says is the cheapest path at this scale ($6-16 per pilot-sized run). Each candidate compiles to a shared object in about 0.3 s [E]. Integer-only code with bounded loops slots straight into the planned integer ABI and the window scheduler, which was bitwise exact in 528 of 528 lives. The evolved program is therefore microcode for the 'one cell processor' the hardware doc proposes, and the per-event instruction budget becomes a cycle budget. HLS or an FPGA tile can run it later. LLM inference runs on someone else's GPUs through an API or a rented open-weights model. Rough budget [E, prices not checked]: 2,000 proposals at about 6k tokens each comes to about $10-300 depending on model tier. Simulation: about 2,000 x 40 lives on average through the cascade, plus about 200 constant-tuning bursts of about 2k lives, at 0.1 CPU-s each, is roughly 15 CPU-h, under one pilot run's 24 CPU-h.
candidates.evidence: FunSearch: new cap-set constructions and bin-packing heuristics better than established baselines, found by LLM program search with an island database and an automatic evaluator. AlphaEvolve: 4x4 complex matrix multiplication with 48 scalar multiplications, the first improvement over Strassen in that setting in 56 years, plus Google data-centre scheduling and accelerator circuit simplifications. ELM: hundreds of thousands of functional Sodarace walker programs (morphology and control as code) in a domain the model had not seen. ShinkaEvolve: state-of-the-art circle packing in about 150 samples. LLM evolution has also found new learning rules: DiscoPOP; Sygkounas 2026 found RL update rules competitive with SAC, PPO, DQN and A2C; OpenArchEvo 2026 evolved spiking architectures as code. Without an LLM, Jordan et al. 2021 evolved compact, interpretable symbolic plasticity rules for spiking networks, and AutoML-Zero rediscovered two-layer networks trained by backprop from primitives. Gaps: none of these evolves a developmental, multicellular, event-driven tissue. Published successes mostly had cheap, low-noise evaluators (my reading of the reported tasks), whereas cell-dev's per-life reliability is 0.026. Not demonstrated at this project's scale.
candidates.risks: (1) Noise. LLM feedback built on noisy F can mislead it. On the other hand, cell-dev needs about 1,000 unpaired lives per arm to see a 0.3 F change but only about 100 to see a 1 F change (2.5 SD) [E]. LLM edits are large, semantic jumps, so they suit a noisy landscape better than the GA's small mutations, but only if they are not mostly destructive, which is unmeasured. (2) Human prior. The LLM tends to write designed roles ('if bottom plane then sensor') and textbook circuits, against the minimal-hard-coding preference. Mitigations: the observable whitelist, energy-charged instructions, and the AutoML-Zero control arm to measure the bias. (3) World exploits. Mitigation: held-out worlds and the existing anti-cheat rules (timer re-placement, c_miss). (4) Code bloat and loss of the 'genetic code' metaphor, because the genome becomes text. Mitigation: GRN as a primitive, and a length penalty. (5) Run-to-run variance and dependence on API model versions. Mitigation: pin model versions and log every prompt and diff for reproducibility.
candidates.prototype: 2 weeks. Week 1: write cell_program.h with EVOLVE-BLOCK handler bodies, the linter, compile-and-load per candidate, and a 'GRN-as-program' seed that reproduces GRN mode bitwise on 64 lives. Hook it into OpenEvolve (or ShinkaEvolve) with 4 islands, the 16/64/256 cascade, CRN seeds, and probe.py summaries in the prompt. Week 2: in SPECK (BODY-1), run 3 seeds x about 1,500 proposals each with a 24 CPU-h simulation budget per seed (one pilot run's budget) and an LLM budget of $100 or less per seed. Run the AutoML-Zero control arm on the same budget. Success: (a) the best program reaches s5's level (+7.06) within that budget in at least 2 of 3 seeds, against the GA median of +4.91 after 500 generations; stretch goal: beat reflex@hollow3 (+8.69) on 1,024 held-out CRN lives. (b) At least one elite gets direction-specific weighting from arrival faces rather than a standing gradient, confirmed by the isotropic-weight knockout. (c) The LLM arm beats the random-mutation arm by more than 2 SE. Kill: after 1,000 proposals, nothing beats the seeded GRN program by more than 0.5 F.
candidates.relaxes: Nothing in the substrate: clockless, event-driven, spikes, one continuous life, local rules and death are all kept. It relaxes 'the genome is a GRN parameter vector' (the genome becomes code with the GRN as one primitive), and it admits a learned human prior into the mutation operator, which is in tension with minimal hard-coding. That tension is measured by the control arm, not assumed away.

candidates.one_liner: Every cell runs the same tiny GRU-like network (the genome), with per-face vector messages and divide and die heads. Population-scale evolution strategies on a GPU tune it across thousands of varied lives, so that within-life adaptation emerges in the cells' states (in-context learning, as in VSML and GPICL) and the same rule runs unchanged at any body size.

candidates.unit: A site holds an alive bit, a hidden state h (16-32 values), an inherited type vector (about 4 values, copied with noise at division, which gives the 'intrinsic state' diversity Nisioti et al. found necessary), and an energy level. All cells share parameters theta, a GRU or tiny MLP-over-history of about 2-20k parameters; theta is the genome. Inputs: 8 per-face message slots (4 values each), the local receptor signal (bottom plane), own energy, and n_view. Outputs: 8 per-face outgoing messages, twitch (act plane), tap, divide logits over faces plus 'none', a die logit, and optionally a per-edge fast-weight update (VSML-style). Weights do not change within a life. Adaptation lives in h (and in the fast weights if used).
candidates.communication: Graded vector messages, one slot per face, so direction is built in rather than made from morphogen chemistry. The lattice is stepped on the GPU, but training randomises each cell's update probability (0.3-0.9 per life) and each edge's delay (1-3 steps), as Growing NCA did with its random update mask, so the rule cannot depend on lockstep. Optional spike-ification: messages pass a learned threshold and are sent only when they change enough (EGRU-style send-on-delta). This restores event-driven, sparse communication and keeps a path to async hardware. Every message costs energy.
candidates.learning: Outer loop: an evolution strategy (OpenAI-ES or SNES in evosax; EGGROLL low-rank perturbations if theta grows) with population 1k-4k. Antithetic pairs share world seeds, the GPU version of CRN. Fitness is F unchanged and one continuous life per evaluation, with no BPTT. ES moves theta along a fitness-weighted average over the whole population, not truncation selection on per-member scores, so per-member Poisson noise is averaged rather than amplified [E]. Inner loop: in-context. Every life draws its world from a distribution (target speed, receptor density, decoys, drag, sensor dropout, later recorded mouse traces), so the only way to score well is to adapt within the life. GPICL suggests state size (cells x hidden size) limits this, which makes growth itself a source of more in-context memory. An optional gradient warm start (BPTT through a differentiable 'expected capture' world, as in NCA training) is possible, but it is a shaped objective, so use it only for pretraining and select on F.
candidates.growth: A fixed maximum tensor (for example 24x24x3 hex-prism sites) with an alive mask. Development starts from one alive cell. Division writes a claim to the chosen face; collisions are resolved at the target by a local hash priority; daughters copy h (or a learned function of it) and get a noisy copy of the type vector. Because theta is shared and local, a rule learned at small body caps runs unchanged at larger ones (the NCA and NDP property). Learning small and expanding is therefore literal: evolve at cap 16-32, then raise the cap and continue evolving the same theta, with no reinitialisation. A cap-transfer score (F at a larger cap with no retraining) is a reported metric. Energy cost per cell and per message keeps growth bounded, as now.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary and multidirectional through per-face messages and recurrent h on every site. Lateral and feedback loops are native. LNDP-style structural plasticity, adding or removing a long-range edge within a capped radius (the user's radius gene), can be added as an output head.
candidates.hardware: Strong fit to current GPUs. Each step is a fixed-index gather of 8 neighbours (a stencil, so effectively a convolution) plus one small GRU on every (life, site), with batch = population x lives x sites in fixed shapes under jit. EvoJAX reports minutes on one accelerator for tasks that took hours or days on CPUs. Rough scale [E]: 1,024 members x 8 lives x 1,728 sites x 2,000 steps x about 20 kFLOP per site-step is about 0.6 PFLOP per generation, which is seconds to tens of seconds on one A100/H100-class GPU. The hardware study estimated a stepped port of the current LIF model at only 2-9x cheaper, because event logic is sparse; a dense recurrent cell is exactly the case GPUs are built for. Later, the frozen theta quantises to int8 and becomes one small MAC array plus state RAM per tile, and EGRU-style thresholded messages give an event-driven chip mapping.
candidates.evidence: Growing NCA: an approximately 8k-parameter shared rule grows and regenerates patterns and was trained with random asynchronous update masks. Variengien et al. 2021: an NCA controlled a cart-pole for hundreds of thousands of iterations and survived input deletion and damage. VSML: a shared tiny LSTM per connection meta-learns learning algorithms that generalise to datasets outside meta-training, with no gradients at test time. GPICL: transformers meta-learn general in-context learners, and state size is the bottleneck. Najarro and Risi 2020 (verified abstract): evolved Hebbian rules let networks with random initial weights adapt within 100 timesteps to morphological damage not seen in training. Pedersen and Risi 2021: sharing rules (61,440 to 1,920 parameters) improved generalisation across 30 morphologies. NDP, LNDP and Nisioti 2024: networks grown by local communication solve control tasks; lateral inhibition is needed to keep diversity; structural plasticity helps under non-stationary reward. Oh et al. 2025: a meta-learned RL update rule beat hand-designed rules on Atari. Gap: none of these combines spiking-like event messages, one continuous life with growth and death, and a body task. The sync-to-async transfer is untested, and cell-dev's v1 collapsed under asynchrony.
candidates.risks: It relaxes spikes (graded vectors) and the clock (stepped training), so it may find algorithms that are lockstep artefacts. The clock-independence gate (cross-cutting) is mandatory. The behaviour is less interpretable than GRN chemistry, though probe-style knockouts still work. ES in about 10k dimensions on Poisson F may need large populations: keep theta small and use CRN. Higher-bandwidth messages may remove the pressure that produced cell-dev's emergent coding tricks (voting, coincidence detection). Meta-learning overfits to its world distribution, so held-out world families are needed. A 2-3 week JAX port of the CATCH world is real engineering, and results will not be bit-comparable with the C kernel.
candidates.prototype: 3 weeks. Week 1: a JAX version of a simplified CATCH (dot body, run-and-tumble blob, receptor pings on the bottom plane, twitch from the act plane, tap from the centre) on a 15x15x2 hex prism, plus the hand-built reflex re-implemented as the yardstick, with a per-site GRU (hidden 16, message 4 per face). Week 2: evosax SNES or OpenAI-ES, population 1,024, 8 lives each, world parameters drawn per life, on one rented L4 or A100 for 2-3 days (about $30-150 [E]). Week 3: gates. Success: (i) at least 50x lives per dollar against the CPU kernel, measured; (ii) beats the re-tuned reflex in the JAX world; (iii) clock-independence: at least 80% of F retained under update probabilities and delay distributions not used in training, and under a fully event-driven re-run in a small CPU reference with jittered local clocks; (iv) cap transfer: theta evolved at cap 32 does not lose F at cap 128, and ideally gains.
candidates.relaxes: Spikes (graded vector messages; spike-ification is optional later) and the global clock during search (stepped GPU updates, made robust by random masks and delays and checked by an async gate). One continuous life is kept under ES; it is relaxed only if the optional gradient warm start is used. It also replaces the GRN chemistry metaphor with a neural cell, although theta is still one shared genome expressed differently in each cell's state. Why it might be worth it: it is the only option here that uses current GPUs and ES at scale on the cell rule itself, and it builds within-life adaptation in, which the user wants for mouse and text worlds.

candidates.unit: Unchanged. Any of today's GRN cell, CellCode or the shared GPU cell. This is a search-side paradigm.
candidates.communication: Unchanged inside the body. Worlds may differ only on the accountant side (ABI section 1: the world reads records and returns only RECEPTOR events), so no generated world can open a global channel into cells. A World ABI linter enforces this, and F stays the task score (no shaped scores, as the review decided).
candidates.learning: Outer loop: 8-16 active pairs, each running the existing GA (or the CellCode loop) for K generations. Every K generations, POET transfer: each pair's elites are tried on the other worlds under CRN and replace residents that score lower. Every pair also keeps a MAP-Elites archive (descriptors: cells at T/2, lateral share, hidden-plane use, growth-stop time), which counters the one-lineage collapse. World generation: v0 is parametric over existing CATCH knobs (twin target, near placement, decoy-lite, sparse receptors, blob speed, field radius). v1: an LLM writes new world modules from the archive of past worlds and their learnability statistics (OMNI-EPIC), for example targets that swap, occlusion bands that need memory, targets that replay recorded human cursor traces, or letter-shaped patterns scrolling across the receptor field. These are kept only if they pass a minimal criterion (some body beats the lone cell by a margin, nothing hits the ceiling) and an OMNI-style 'interesting and not a near-duplicate' judgement. Optional ASAL-style novelty: embed atlas raster images with a vision-language model to find behaviourally new bodies. Inner loop: whatever the substrate provides.
candidates.growth: Field radius and receptor sparsity are world axes. A bigger field rewards more sensory coverage, so bodies must grow. Transfers carry algorithms evolved on small fields into large-field worlds, where selection extends them: learn small, expand on growth, with the expansion pressure coming from the environment rather than a hard-coded size schedule. Memory-demanding worlds (occlusion, delayed tap) give hidden planes a job, which the reactive SPECK world does not (hidden_off changed F by at most +0.04).
candidates.circuitry: Substrate-dependent. The contribution is pressure, not a mechanism: worlds needing integration over distance and time reward lateral and feedback loops, and depth.
candidates.hardware: Embarrassingly parallel on the CPU boxes cell-dev already uses (pairs are independent; transfers are batched evaluations). LLM world-writing is a few hundred calls, which is cheap. If the world moves to the GPU (candidate 2), Kinetix/Jax2D shows procedurally generated 2D physics worlds at billions of steps on accelerators.
candidates.evidence: POET: many generated challenges were solved only through transfer between pairs, not by direct optimisation or a fixed curriculum. Enhanced POET adds a domain-general novelty measure (PATA-EC) and an open-endedness metric. OMNI and OMNI-EPIC: foundation models generate environments plus reward code and choose learnable, interesting next tasks. ASAL: CLIP-guided search found new lifeforms and open-ended CAs in Lenia, Boids, Particle Life, Game of Life and NCA. Kinetix: an agent trained on procedurally generated 2D physics tasks solved unseen human-designed ones zero-shot. Darwin Godel Machine: archive-based open-ended search raised SWE-bench from 20.0% to 50.0%. Project evidence that worlds matter: the router leads by +2.2 F in base SPECK, by about 0 with a twin target, near placement or decoy-lite, and by -1.28 with sparse receptors. Every run collapses to one breed by generation 2-119, and the founder screen does not predict the winner. Gap: none of the cited systems used growing multicellular bodies, and published POET-family runs used large compute.
candidates.risks: Compute is split across many worlds, so each pair gets fewer generations, and transfer tests under Poisson noise are costly (use the cascade and CRN). LLM-written worlds may hide shaped rewards, leaks or exploits (linter, plus a human or reviewer pass on each accepted world). 'Interesting' as judged by an LLM is a human prior. Open-ended loops are hard to judge: pre-register a held-out world panel. It could drift into worlds that reward trivial reflexes. Keep a minimal criterion that requires lateral messages (for example, worlds where lateral_off must cost F).
candidates.prototype: 2 weeks. Week 1: v0 parametric POET over CATCH knobs: 8 pairs x population 64, transfers every 25 generations, per-world MAP-Elites archives, random tie-breaking, 3 seeds, about 3x a pilot run's CPU (about 75 CPU-h, under $15 on a rented box [E from HARDWARE_PATH rates]). Week 2: an LLM world writer constrained by the World ABI linter, 20 generated worlds, minimal-criterion filtering. Success, at equal total CPU against single-world SPECK GA on a pre-registered held-out panel of 6 worlds (including sparse receptors and a cursor-trace world), all with paired CRN lives: (a) the archive's best generalist beats the single-world champion on mean F; (b) at least 3 distinct breeds survive at the end; (c) at least one logged transfer gives a gain that the source pair's own lineage had not reached.
candidates.relaxes: None of the substrate preferences. It relaxes the single fixed task and the single population per run, and it adds LLM priors in world design, not in cells. The user already wants much more task variety for generalisation, and the review's niche map of worlds is a first step toward this.

candidates.name: Predictive tissue: every cell is a tiny local world model that learns during the life; evolution designs development and the learning rule (Baldwinian)
candidates.one_liner: Give each cell a small predictor of its own next inputs (neighbour messages and receptor), trained online by a purely local error-driven rule. Messages carry predictions one way and surprises the other. Daughters inherit their mother's learned weights, and evolution acts only on the developmental program and the learning rule's coefficients.
inspiration: Loewe S, O'Connor P, Veeling BS (2019, NeurIPS). Putting An End to End-to-End: Gradient-Isolated Learning of Representations (Greedy InfoMax: local self-supervised losses per module, asynchronous optimisation). https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.11786
Millidge B, Tschantz A, Buckley CL (2020). Predictive Coding Approximates Backprop along Arbitrary Computation Graphs (local Hebbian updates). https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04182

Bellec G, Scherr F, Subramoney A, ..., Maass W (2020, Nature Communications). A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons (e-prop). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y (metadata via Europe PMC only)
Najarro E, Risi S (2020). Meta-Learning through Hebbian Plasticity in Random Networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.02686
Hinton GE, Nowlan SJ (1987). How Learning Can Guide Evolution. Complex Systems 1(3). https://www.complex-systems.com/abstracts/v01_i03_a06/
Chen T, Goodfellow I, Shlens J (2016, ICLR). Net2Net: Accelerating Learning via Knowledge Transfer (function-preserving growth). https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05641
Subramoney A et al. (2023, ICLR). EGRU: threshold-triggered event communication. https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06178
Plantec E et al. (2024). LNDP: plasticity driven by spontaneous activity before experience. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09787
Jordan J, Schmidt M, Senn W, Petrovici MA (2021, eLife). Evolving to learn: interpretable plasticity rules for spiking networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14149
candidates.unit: A cell holds state h and a small plastic predictor W (linear, or a 2-layer model with about 100-500 weights). At each local update it predicts its next input vector (per-face incoming signals plus receptor) from h, and computes the local error e = x - prediction. Learning rule: dW = eta * gate * (e outer h) - decay * W. The coefficients (eta, decay, gating by own energy or neuromodulator, and which inputs are predicted) are evolved, or written by CellCode, in the style of Jordan et al. 2021, not hand-fixed. Act cells turn predictions into twitches and taps (for example, act toward where the receptor field predicts the target will be), or through an evolved readout. A capture event delivered at the tap cell spreads as a local neuromodulator packet and serves as the third factor for the action pathway (e-prop-like, but local).
candidates.communication: Bidirectional by construction: predictions flow toward the sensory plane, and errors (surprises) flow away from it, on any lattice graph, not only in layers (predictive coding works on arbitrary computation graphs). Errors are sent as events only when |e| exceeds an evolved threshold (send-on-delta, EGRU-style), so communication stays sparse and can stay event-driven and clockless in the C kernel. Graded payloads relax value-less spikes, but a 1-bit 'surprise up/down' spike version is a natural variant to test.
candidates.learning: Inner loop (within the one continuous life): local error-driven weight learning in every cell, with no global backward pass and no global learning signal. It is local self-supervision plus a locally diffused reward. Outer loop: the existing GA (or CellCode, or ES) evolves the developmental program, the learning-rule coefficients and the initial W priors. This is the Baldwin effect (Hinton and Nowlan 1987): learning reshapes the fitness landscape, which can soften the parent-to-child loss and raise selection's reliability, since a body that learns is less sensitive to small genomic changes [hypothesis to test].
candidates.growth: At division the daughter copies its mother's learned W (plus small noise) and h. Expansion therefore preserves function, like Net2Net, and literally carries local optimizations learned while the body was small into the newly grown tissue within the same life. Across generations, evolution keeps the developmental rules that grow bodies whose learned optimizations transfer well as they grow. Growth also adds prediction capacity where errors stay high, which could be a local growth trigger ('divide where you are persistently surprised') that evolution may or may not keep.
candidates.circuitry: Arbitrary and multidirectional: every edge carries both predictions and errors, and recurrent loops are the norm. A capped radius gene could add longer edges.
candidates.hardware: On a GPU (stepped), every update is a per-site small matmul plus a local outer-product update, batched across sites and lives with no BPTT and no global gradient, so memory is O(state), not O(time). The event-driven C kernel can run it too, since all updates are per-site and triggered by arrivals or ticks. For a chip, on-chip local learning without weight transport is the standard neuromorphic goal, and it fits the integer ABI if W is quantised (a precision study is needed; the gene state already needs 10 or more fractional bits).
candidates.evidence: Greedy InfoMax: purely local self-supervised losses built competitive representations, and modules can be optimised asynchronously. Predictive coding with only local Hebbian updates converges to backprop gradients on arbitrary computation graphs (CNNs, RNNs and LSTMs matched backprop). e-prop: recurrent spiking networks learn with eligibility traces and learning signals. Najarro and Risi 2020: evolved local Hebbian rules adapt random networks within 100 steps to unseen damage. Hinton and Nowlan 1987: learning can guide evolution (Baldwin effect). Net2Net: function-preserving widening and deepening. Gap: no demonstration of local predictive learning inside a growing, dying, single-life tissue that controls a body. The coupling between learned prediction and reward-driven action is the open part.
candidates.risks: Collapse to trivial predictions (constant or copying the input); needs noise or contrastive targets. The local objective may not align with F (good predictors that do not catch). Online learning in a recurrent lattice can be unstable (needs homeostatic decay, which is evolvable). The form of the learning rule is a hard-coded choice, in tension with minimal hard-coding; mitigate by evolving its coefficients and terms (CellCode). Graded messages relax spikes. It is most natural for the user's later prediction tasks (cursor following, text fill-in) and may add little to the reactive SPECK task.
candidates.prototype: 1-2 weeks, stepped NumPy/JAX or a CPU fork of program mode. World: a cursor-prediction variant of CATCH in which the target moves with smooth correlated dynamics (later, recorded human mouse traces) and a capture requires tapping where the target will be. Arms, at an equal evolution budget: learning on with weight inheritance; learning on without inheritance; learning off (evolution only). Add a mid-life switch of target dynamics. Success: (a) learning-on beats learning-off by more than 2 SE on held-out dynamics; (b) F recovers after the mid-life switch within a fixed fraction of the life; (c) the benefit grows with body size (inheritance arm better than no-inheritance at large caps), which shows learned local optimizations expanding with growth; (d) parent-to-child F loss is smaller than in the learning-off arm (the Baldwin signal).
candidates.relaxes: Value-less spikes (graded or thresholded error events; a 1-bit variant is possible). It adds within-life weight change, a new fixed mechanism that needs the user's approval under minimal hard-coding; its form is made evolvable. The clock is relaxed only in a stepped GPU version; the event-driven CPU version keeps clocklessness and the one continuous life. Why it might be worth it: it is the most direct reading of 'learn local optimizations while smaller and expand them on growth', and it fits the planned mouse-cursor and text-stream worlds, which are prediction problems.

explored.cross_cutting: 1) Spend lives where they decide something, and never change F. Use a cascade under common random numbers (16, then 64, then 256 lives; successive halving or racing) for every candidate a search produces. Optionally add a learned surrogate (genome or code embedding plus early-life features), used only to decide which candidates get more lives and never as the selection score. OpenArchEvo 2026 used surrogate prediction this way. This respects the review's rejection of shaped scores (distance and time-near-target are 10-17x more heritable than F but predict F worse). 2) Diversity by construction: islands with ring migration (FunSearch, OpenEvolve), per-world MAP-Elites archives, and archive-based parent choice (Darwin Godel Machine) against the measured collapse to one breed by generation 2-119, together with the already-planned random tie-breaking. 3) Function-preserving expansion as a standard mutation class: gene duplication, a new handler branch, a new message channel or a new plane starts out with zero effect or as a split copy (Net2Net), and a regression gate requires a child to keep about 90% of its parent's F on the parent's world before it is scored on a larger world or body cap. This makes 'learn small, expand later' explicit and avoids the 0.19 F loss per random child. 4) Two timescales in every loop: rare structural jumps (LLM edits, new genes, new worlds) and frequent cheap numeric tuning (GA, CMA-ES or ES on constants). Large semantic jumps suit a noisy landscape: about 100 lives detect a 1 F change, while about 1,000 per arm are needed for 0.3 F [E, from SD 2.5]. 5) A clock-independence gate lets search relax the clock without giving up the property. Any rule found in stepped form (GPU, NCA-style) must keep at least 80% of its F when re-run under randomised update probabilities and delays not seen in training, and finally in the exact event-driven kernel with jittered local clocks (tick_jit exists). Search can be synchronous; the accepted results must not depend on it. 6) One reference contract for hardware: whatever wins (an LLM-written program, a shared GRU, a predictive cell) is compiled into the planned integer ABI and replayed bitwise with the window scheduler, and EGRU-style send-on-delta messages keep it event-driven. The cell's per-event instruction budget, charged as energy, doubles as the hardware cycle budget. 7) Feed cell-dev's diagnostics back to the search: probe.py knockouts, lineage tables and lateral_off and hidden_off deltas are exactly the 'reflection' text that Eureka- and ReEvo-style LLM loops use; few projects have such mechanistic feedback ready-made. 8) The Baldwin effect as a design lever: any within-life adaptation (in-context state in candidate 2, local predictive learning in candidate 4, plasticity written in CellCode) is expected to smooth the landscape that evolution searches (Hinton & Nowlan 1987). Measure it as a smaller parent-to-child F loss and a higher per-life reliability, not only as higher F. 9) Suggested order: CellCode first (keeps every substrate preference, reuses the C kernel and probe tooling, and targets the review's main levers: direction-specific input, large informed mutations, islands). Then the parametric POET wrapper (cheap, CPU-only, aimed at generalisation and lineage collapse). Then the GPU in-context cell as the scaling bet, and the predictive tissue when the cursor and text worlds arrive. Candidate 1's LLM can also write candidate 4's learning-rule coefficients and terms, and candidate 3's world writer can serve any substrate.

judged.judge: Fidelity judge. I scored against the user's goals: a body learns local optimisations while small and keeps and extends them as it grows; evolution does the search; circuits can run in any direction; local rules with emergent roles rather than designed ones; bio-inspired; later tasks (steering, mouse, text) and generalisation; and the project can still answer "what local algorithms emerge?". The two binding clarifications are weighted inside every score. First, the organism's own runtime must run natively on hardware and the training simulator must match that runtime closely (small sim-to-hardware gap). Second, visible outcomes must come cheaply and quickly. Repo checks: per-face weights already exist in the kernel (src/life/kernel.c:201, weff[DMAX][2], summed on arrival at :1063). RESULTS.md confirms that apoptosis is never used and hidden planes are inert (hidden_off at most +0.04). So the claims that plastic faces are cheap to add, and that depth and death need a job, are grounded. New citations were opened or checked for this verdict: Hasani et al. 2021 CfC (arXiv opened), Cranmer et al. 2020 (arXiv opened), Chen et al. 2019 Learning by Cheating (arXiv opened), Bhatia et al. 2021 Evolution Gym (arXiv opened). Two were checked through Crossref metadata only: Lechner et al. 2020 NCP and Medvet et al. 2020. Web search was exhausted, so I could do no broader search.

scores.name: A. Plastic faces: evolved three-factor STDP on per-face synapses, inherited at division (keeps the clockless kernel)
scores.why: Highest fidelity of all 19. Learned per-face weights are copied into daughters, which is the literal form of 'learn small, keep on growth'.
